#5635. Fellow Physicians, Let AI Fill in the Blanks

— This new technology can make it easier to get it all done

A few weeks ago, I saw a patient for a regularly scheduled follow-up for a problem they'd been having, and they told me they were scheduled to see a specialist to address this problem the following week.

When I looked through my schedule at the patient's chart that day, I noticed there was already a note for that date in the future that had been created a few days earlier. Curious, I opened the note up to see what it contained.

Had the patient been mistaken or had I misunderstood? Had they already seen this specialist?

The note was apparently authored by a member of that specialist's office staff, and seemed to be a nearly completely fleshed-out office visit record addressing the problem, except for a few placeholder stars (***) that apparently were what was going to be added on the day of the actual visit.

"This patient with a past medical history of X, Y, and Z presents with a complaint of *** that has been going on for *** days, at its worst *** out of 10 in intensity, radiating to their ***, made worse by ***, alleviated by ***."

Then there was a lot of other templated material pulled from the patient's chart, including their chart-noted past medical history, past surgical history, social history, medications, allergies, and the results of recent labs and several relevant imaging studies.

At the end there was an assessment and plan: "The patient presents with *** and the following options were offered to the patient, ***, ***, ***. The risks, benefits, and alternatives of *** were discussed with the patient, including the following potential outcomes and the patient wishes to proceed."

You get the picture -- fill in the blanks.

With the incredible amount of documentation we're required to do, shortcuts and ways to make things easier are definitely a good thing. In most cases, no one really reads the charts that carefully, but it is useful to have it all there so that critical information can be ascertained and so we all know what is going on.

In our electronic medical record, there are some amazing tools (and seemingly more every week), including ambient listening that crunches our conversations with patients and turns them into medical text, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted responses to patient portal messages, and form fillers that can churn out a printed copy of standard medical forms.

As we keep building on these systems, and finding more sophisticated ways to make the lives of our patients and our own lives better -- especially freeing us up from administrative tasks that don't need clinical brainpower -- I'm hopeful the rest of this rote stuff will fall away, and that the documentation and everything else that needs to be done can happen smoothly and quickly.

I envision a day when really smart predictive and generative AI systems will be listening along, working by our sides, making sure we don't miss anything, and helping us accomplish all the administrative and bureaucratic tasks heaped upon us. It may even help us with clinical decision-making, ordering tests as necessary, interpreting follow-up results, generating patient instructions, refilling prescriptions.

While I'm sitting there and discussing the patient's medical condition and our plan, it's nice that right now, ambient listening turns that into the patient's History of Present Illness for my office note. But it would also be great if it generated something that could be popped into the After Visit Summary, instructions for the patients to take home.

When I mention the lab testing I want to get, rechecking their cholesterol to see response to a statin, getting electrolytes after newly starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, rechecking their hemoglobin A1c for ongoing monitoring of their diabetes, the orders should be entered in the system at the same time as I say these words, associated with the correct medical condition and thus the correct diagnosis code, and queued up for me to review and sign.

I never want any of this to be autonomous, running on its own, practicing medicine. But there are so many opportunities for this to safely take a leap, to truly make our healthcare system more equitable and more efficient and, believe it or not, more caring.

Patients shouldn't have to struggle to get a form completed, to get a refill of their chronic medications, to get a follow-up referral to a specialist they have been seeing for an ongoing medical condition, to order their mammogram or colonoscopy or flu shot or shingles vaccine.

Never take us out of the loop but use this new technology to make it easier for us to take care of them, to get it all done.

#5633. The Permanente Medical Group launches tech incubation company

The Permanente Medical Group launches tech incubation company" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Permanente Medical Group announced on Monday the launch of a physician-led innovation company it said will strike technology partnerships to co-develop, incubate and launch new enterprise healthcare delivery technologies.

Permanentech—a wholly owned subsidiary of the 10,000-physician medical group, which is itself part of the massive integrated nonprofit Kaiser Permanente—looks to rapidly advance potential new healthcare offerings informed by its frontline physicians and the broader organization’s focus on value-based care.

It marked the launch by announcing its first portfolio company: Wrapt Health, which offers an automated tool that predicts likely missed medical appointments for early outreach and rescheduling. In line with Permanentech’s broader thesis, it was born from a TPMG physician’s experiences, validated within the medical group and so far scaled to 22 sites in Kaiser Permanente’s Northern California region.

“Our clinicians are continuously innovating and refining how we deliver care,” Kenneth Trauner, M.D., CEO of Permanentech and chief innovation officer at TPMG, said in a release. “Permanentech gives them a dedicated resource to rapidly turn their insights and creativity into scalable solutions that benefit both our patients and the wider health care community.”

Permanentech will be focused on technologies and AI-enabled tools addressing patient service, access and quality, TPMG said, with successful products also having the potential to improve “the economics of care delivery.” The business is structured “to move at the pace of the technology industry,” but has “a clear advantage” via its access to TPMG and Kaiser Permanente’s substantial footprint for deployment and validation, it said.

Those efforts will involve both home-grown tools and those developed by established or early-stage partners.

The former will champion physician-developed tools created inside TPMG’s ecosystem as an independent company launches. Starting from the concept phase, that support would include financing as well as clinical and operational validation, as was the case with Wrapt Health.

“Our physicians and care teams see every day where technology can make care better,” Kristine Lee, M.D., an associate executive director and chief transformation officer at TPMG, said. “Permanentech gives them a real hand in building tools that lift administrative burden and give time back to patients. When clinicians help build the tools, those tools fit the way they actually work.”

Strategic partnerships and joint ventures, meanwhile, will focus on co-development, clinical valuation and scaled deployment. Permanentech said the latter will begin with local deployments that are expanded to other TPMG sites when solutions “prove their value,” and could include additional strategic support as a partner company looks to advance their offering beyond TPMG.

Permanentech plans to add more portfolio companies and partnerships “in the coming months,” according to its announcement.

“For decades, our physicians have delivered high-quality, preventive care inside an integrated system where clinical expertise, data and incentives all point toward keeping people healthy,” Maria Ansari, M.D., CEO and executive director of TPMG, said. “Permanentech is our commitment to putting that ecosystem to work alongside the best technology from inside and outside our walls.”

Pleasanton, California-based TPMG is the country’s largest medical group, caring for 4.7 million Northern California members with about 10,000 physicians and nearly 47,000 nurses and support staff. It operates at 203 medical offices and facilities, as well as 21 hospitals.

Its parent organization, Kaiser Permanente, is the country’s largest nonprofit health system by operating revenue ($127.7 billion in 2025). Topline financial results shared earlier this month outlined a 9% year-over-year increase in Q3 operating revenue, while the system’s Risant Health value-based care platform subsidiary in October announced plans to acquire Integris Health, Oklahoma’s largest nonprofit provider.

#5632. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5631. Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk

Your daily cup of coffee may be doing more than helping you wake up in the morning. A long-running study of U.S. adults suggests that drinking caffeinated coffee regularly is associated with a substantially lower risk of dementia and better cognitive health as people age.

Researchers found that adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee developed dementia at considerably lower rates than those who rarely or never drank it. The findings were based on follow-up periods extending as long as 43 years, offering a valuable look at how everyday drinking habits relate to brain health over time.

The strongest associations appeared among people who drank two to three cups of caffeinated coffee each day. Tea consumption was also linked to better cognitive outcomes, although the amount associated with the greatest benefit was somewhat lower.

Interestingly, decaffeinated coffee did not show the same benefits, raising questions about whether caffeine itself might help explain the connection.

Coffee Drinkers Showed Much Lower Dementia Rates

One of the most striking findings involved the difference in dementia rates between regular coffee drinkers and people who consumed little or no coffee.

Among U.S. adults who drank higher amounts of caffeinated coffee, researchers recorded 141 dementia cases annually for every 100,000 people. In comparison, the rate was 330 cases per 100,000 people each year among those who rarely or never drank caffeinated coffee.

Dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with memory, thinking, reasoning, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer's disease is its most common cause, although several other brain disorders can also lead to dementia.

While occasional forgetfulness can be a normal part of aging, dementia involves cognitive difficulties severe enough to disrupt daily life. Identifying lifestyle habits associated with lower dementia risk is therefore an important area of research, particularly as populations grow older.

The findings suggest that regular caffeinated coffee consumption may be one such habit. However, the results show an association rather than proving that coffee directly prevents dementia. Other differences between coffee drinkers and people who avoid coffee could also contribute to the observed results.

Coffee Was Also Linked to Better Cognitive Health

The potential benefits were not limited to diagnosed dementia. Participants who drank more caffeinated coffee were also less likely to report that their memory or thinking abilities had declined.

Researchers found that 7.8% of adults who consumed higher amounts of caffeinated coffee reported subjective cognitive decline, compared with 9.5% of those who rarely or never drank it.

Subjective cognitive decline refers to changes in memory or thinking that people notice themselves, even when those difficulties have not necessarily been confirmed by formal cognitive testing. Someone experiencing it might feel that remembering information, concentrating, or finding the right words has become more difficult.

Such complaints do not automatically indicate dementia. Nevertheless, they can provide useful information about how people perceive changes in their cognitive abilities as they grow older.

The lower percentage among caffeinated coffee drinkers adds to the evidence linking coffee consumption with healthier cognitive aging.

How Much Coffee Offers the Greatest Benefit?

The researchers also examined whether the amount of coffee consumed was related to the strength of the observed benefits.

Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was associated with the most favorable outcomes for dementia risk and cognitive functioning.

Notably, this association remained apparent regardless of participants' genetic risk of developing dementia. In other words, the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health was observed even among people whose inherited characteristics might make them more vulnerable to the disease.

Genetic risk refers to the influence of inherited variations in DNA that can increase or decrease a person's likelihood of developing certain conditions. Although genetics can play an important role in dementia, they are only one part of a much larger picture that includes age, general health, and lifestyle.

The results also suggest that drinking larger amounts of coffee is not necessarily better. Consumption beyond the range associated with the strongest benefits did not appear to provide additional protection.

Tea Drinkers May Benefit Too, but Decaf Was Different

Coffee was not the only beverage associated with better brain health. Researchers found that drinking tea was also linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning.

For tea, the strongest associations appeared among participants who consumed one to two cups per day. As with coffee, drinking more than this amount did not appear to produce further benefits.

However, the study did not distinguish between caffeinated and noncaffeinated tea. As a result, the findings cannot establish whether caffeine was responsible for the association observed among tea drinkers.

The results for coffee offered an additional clue. While regular caffeinated coffee was associated with lower dementia risk and better cognitive outcomes, decaffeinated coffee did not demonstrate the same benefits.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea, and several other plants. It acts on the central nervous system and is best known for temporarily increasing alertness and reducing feelings of tiredness.

Whether caffeine also contributes to better brain health over many years is a separate question. The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating, but it does not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.

Taken together, the findings suggest that moderate consumption of caffeinated coffee and tea may be associated with healthier brain aging. For coffee drinkers, two to three cups daily appeared to offer the strongest association, while one to two cups of tea showed the most favorable results among tea drinkers.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these beverages directly influence dementia risk, the long-term findings offer encouraging news for people who already enjoy coffee or tea as part of their daily routine.

Margaret is a Washington correspondent covering the Food and Drug Administration and other federal health agencies. Reach her on Signal at margaretmanto.61.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration is proposing a new classification for a product that’s existed in a legal gray area for years, a win for proponents of dietary supplements, including members of the MAHA movement.

The proposed rule would classify N-acetyl-L-cysteine, known as NAC and already widely sold over the counter, as the agency’s first “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition” — in essence, not not a supplement.

The need for the legal backbending stems from the fact that the FDA previously approved NAC as a drug, and FDA regulations prohibit the agency from including approved drugs in the dietary supplement category. In 1963, the agency approved NAC to break up mucus in certain lung conditions, and in 1985 to treat acetaminophen overdose.

#5629. How Impactful Is Stock Epinephrine for Anaphylaxis at Schools?

— Survey of school nurses suggests failure with relying on students to carry autoinjectors

Most schools that keep a stock epinephrine autoinjector available to treat allergic reactions also require children with known severe allergies to bring their own, a survey of school nurses found.

While 87% of their schools carried stock epinephrine, 71.3% of these still required students to bring a personal supply, reported Mahi K. Singh, MD, of University of Chicago Medicine, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (ACAAI) annual meeting.

With 10% of nurses reporting an emergency when epinephrine was not available for a student who needed it, schools without stock were 4.42 times more likely to report epinephrine unavailability when needed compared with schools that did have it (P<0.001).

All U.S. states now have laws that authorize students with severe allergies to carry and self-administer epinephrine. By 2023, all but four had laws to allow or require schools to stock emergency supplies of epinephrine autoinjectors.

"In anaphylactic emergency, having stock is extremely helpful, even if the school is also requiring personal supply," Singh told MedPage Today. However, "there's a lot of overlap suggesting potentially a lot of excess supply," she said, pointing to a high rate of unused, expired autoinjectors.

"That's also underscored by the fact that epinephrine use in schools is infrequent," Singh added. Almost three-quarters of schools reported no epinephrine administration in the past year, from either personal supply or stock; 97.0% never used more than two epinephrine devices in a single day.

Despite this excess supply, most nurses surveyed (73.6%) said they still favor a dual-coverage model over stock-only supply.

"Our thought was that potentially we could switch or propose switching to a stock-only model to prevent some of this excess or unused supply," Singh said. "It would be more cost effective, and also it would reduce administrative burden on students and families and school nurses. But there remains this discomfort with moving to a stock-only model ... So that definitely needs some more exploration, because nurses know what's happening in schools more than any of us do."

Stock epinephrine doesn't help if there are no school nurses or they don't feel comfortable administering it, commented Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

Newer forms of epinephrine might help both with hesitancy and other obstacles, he said. "A teacher may be much more willing to do a nose spray on a kid or drop a little film under the kid's tongue rather than jab him with an autoinjector."

The approved nasal epinephrine spray (neffy), a sublingual film he presented data on at the conference, and a nasal dry powder all show better stability data than the autoinjectors, both withstanding freezing and then thawing as well as higher temperatures before degrading, Lieberman said.

And whereas an autoinjector might have an expiration date a year from purchase, the nasal spray lasts typically 2 years, he said. "That helps out a school ... Less changing out of the device if they ever were to stock it. And obviously our patients, because if they don't use it lasts them longer."

The cross-sectional survey presented by Singh was distributed to a national database of 1,847 U.S. school nurses from August through December 2025. The 349 nurses who responded (18.9% response rate) represented 31 states, although almost 40% came from Illinois, where the University of Chicago holds an annual conference for school nurses. Nearly all of the nurses came from public schools (90.8%), with an average of 762 students per school.

Limitations of the study included the low response rate, the outsized influence on the results of Illinois policies, and unknown generalizability to schools that don't have a dedicated school nurse.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's plans to combine have earned the blessing of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a key hurdle that paves the path for a Jan. 1, 2027 close.

The nonprofit systems and the attorney general's office announced Monday an oversight agreement replete with service line preservation requirements and $2.15 billion of promised capital investments. Their deal is set to create a 39-hospital cross-regional health system that would be a major player in Minnesota's increasingly concentrated healthcare market.

"My office has extensive authority to review healthcare transactions in Minnesota: we take it very seriously and with every review, we apply the lens of whether it will help you afford your life and live with dignity, safety and respect," Ellison said in the announcement. "At the end of our thorough review of the transaction between Sutter and Allina, I have determined it passes the public-interest test.”

Per the attorney general's office, the $2.5 billion be invested over five years to increase healthcare capacity in the state. That includes $150 million toward rural care, $50 million in workforce development and the scaling of virtual addiction therapy programs across the state.

The systems also agreed to maintain core services at rural locations for five years, to maintain reproductive and gender care for five years (as it complies with state and federal statute) and to continue Medicare participation and charity care. For Allina's workforce, they also agreed to retain all employees in good standing, honor all collective bargaining agreements and not enforce some noncompete agreements.

Ellison's office will enforce the five-year commitments via a 10-year period of oversight, which will include annual compliance reports from Sutter and Allina.

"In the context where the provision of healthcare everywhere is under serious financial strain and Allina is facing its own struggles, I appreciate that Sutter is entering Minnesota with a mindset of growth and an understanding that we cannot simply cut our way out of financial challenges and maintain Minnesota’s high standard of healthcare," Ellison said. "Sutter’s leadership has a history of delivering on growth and innovation and I look forward to their doing the same here."

Since the nonprofits announced their deal back in March, Minnesota and the Midwest have been the stage for substantial health system dealmaking. Sanford Health announced and closed its acquisition of North Memorial Health, while Essentia Health and HealthPartners in September shared new plans to combine and form an integrated 22-hospital organization.

Sutter and Allina, in a joint statement, thanked Ellison's office for the sign-off and said they plan to close their transaction on Jan. 1, 2027.

"From the beginning, our vision has been grounded in a simple yet powerful belief: people across Minnesota and western Wisconsin deserve a sustainable health system that provides access to high-quality, affordable health care when and where they need it," the statement reads. "With our combined capabilities and more than $2 billion in investment, we will expand access to care, improve affordability, enhance care team and patient experiences and accelerate high-impact research and innovation."

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's pending combination took a step forward this week with the signing of a definitive agreement, the nonprofit systems announced Thursday.

The agreement locks in the plans shared earlier this year in a letter of intent—namely, that the cross-market deal would bring more than $2 billion of investment to Allina's markets and that the smaller system would become the "Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health."

Now the organizations are left with securing state and federal regulatory approvals before the deal can close, which they expect to happen before the end of this year.

“This important milestone brings us one step closer to our goal of partnering to enhance care, support our teams and expand clinical capabilities and research as a strong, nonprofit health system,” Lisa Shannon, president and CEO of Allina Health, said in Thursday's announcement. “With our combined expertise, complementary strengths and aligned missions and visions, I am confident we will be well-positioned to meet the evolving needs of our patients and communities now and well into the future.

Should the deal close, the resulting organization would span 39 hospitals as well as more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The organization would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health unveiled plans to join and form a 39-hospital, $26 billion nonprofit health system.

The pair said Tuesday that they have signed a letter of intent for Allina to join Sutter. Allina would maintain its brand and regional headquarters but operate as the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter. Under that arrangement, Sutter is also committing $2 billion to bolster care access and patient experience investments in Allina’s Minnesota and western Wisconsin markets.

“This includes establishing new ambulatory and specialty care sites to fill care gaps and meet growing community needs, as well as recruiting more physicians and enhancing AI and digital health capabilities,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas, who would maintain those titles should the deal close, said in the announcement. “Building on our complementary strengths and combined expertise, we will build a healthcare innovation engine that accelerates how ideas move from development and design into improving the health of patients and communities.”

The systems said they plan to complete due diligence and finalize terms for a definitive agreement “over the coming weeks and months,” targeting a close before the end of 2026 should regulatory reviews run smoothly. A representative for Allina described the structure of the proposed agreement as being similar to a member substitution but noted that the deal's final structure will be outlined in the pending definitive agreement.

Alongside the 39 hospitals, the resulting organization would include more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The combination would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Among the benefits of their proposed partnership, the systems led their announcement with the synergistic technical expertise of their organizations and surrounding communities: Sutter’s immersion in Northern California's artificial intelligence and platform development and Allina’s seat in the medtech and engineering hub of Minnesota.

“The proposed combined system will be uniquely positioned to be a national leader in digital and technological advancements that meaningfully improve patients’ and caregivers’ experiences, while continuing to provide the compassionate care their respective communities have relied on for decades,” the announcement reads.

Such efforts, outlined in the announcement, include AI and digital solutions that would reduce administrative burdens for caregivers along with more convenient appointment scheduling for patients via digital consumer tools.

More broadly, the organizations said they expect the combination will help the organizations bolster physician and clinician recruitment, improve patient affordability and grow their capabilities, “particularly in clinical centers of excellence.”

“We are incredibly excited for the opportunity to harness the collective strength of our two mission-driven organizations to make a difference in the lives of our patients, communities and care teams,” said Allina Health President and CEO Lisa Shannon, who would also maintain those titles in regard to the to-be-formed Upper Midwest Division. “As one nationally leading, locally committed nonprofit health system, we will be uniquely positioned to be at the forefront of innovation, building upon the expertise of our physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses and team members to chart a new path for healthcare.”

Twenty-seven-hospital Sutter is the larger of the two organizations, with $19.8 billion reported total revenue and a $509 million operating income in 2025 (excluding impacts of the to-be-approved 2025 Hospital Fee Program). In the past year, it opened 31 additional care sites, added more than 1,100 physicians and reached 3.6 million patients.

Allina reports $6 billion of revenue with a $95.4 million operating loss and has not had a positive operating margin for the past few years. It operates 12 hospitals and more than 100 other sites.

#5627. Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins

A major clinical trial has raised new questions about how doctors decide who should take statins to prevent heart attacks and strokes. Researchers found that using heart scans to guide treatment decisions produced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, even though the scans led to far fewer recommendations to begin taking statins.

The findings, presented during a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026, also revealed a striking difference in how consistently patients took their medication. Those advised to use statins based on calcium buildup in their coronary arteries were substantially more likely to follow their treatment recommendations.

Although the results suggest that heart scans could help doctors make more targeted treatment decisions, the trial did not establish that the scan approach was as effective as conventional risk assessment. Researchers say additional studies are needed to determine whether it offers a better strategy for preventing cardiovascular disease.

Why Predicting Heart Disease Risk Remains a Challenge

Cardiovascular disease remains the world's leading cause of illness and death. Much of this burden comes from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), which develops when fatty deposits known as plaque accumulate inside arteries, restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke are two major forms of this condition.

Several common factors increase the likelihood of developing ASCVD, including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and elevated cholesterol. Doctors use these factors to estimate a person's cardiovascular risk and determine whether preventive medications are appropriate.

Statins are among the most widely used treatments for lowering that risk. These medications reduce cholesterol levels, particularly low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called LDL or bad cholesterol. They also help lower the likelihood of serious cardiovascular complications.

However, identifying which patients stand to benefit from statins remains a significant challenge. Some people who eventually experience a heart attack do not appear to be at particularly high risk under conventional screening methods.

"For far too many patients, the first symptom of ASCVD is a heart attack," said Doctor Joseph B Muhlestein from the Intermountain Medical Center, Murray, USA, the Principal Investigator of the CorCal Outcomes trial. "Statins have been shown to be highly effective in the prevention of ASCVD; however, there is a major gap in risk assessment, statin initiation, and statin persistence."

According to Muhlestein, many people who suffer their first heart attack, particularly younger adults, would not previously have been classified as having enough cardiovascular risk to justify statin treatment. This limitation has prompted researchers to investigate whether directly examining the arteries might provide more useful information.

Can Heart Calcium Scans Improve Statin Decisions?

The CorCal Outcomes trial investigated two different approaches for determining which patients should be advised to begin statin therapy before experiencing a cardiovascular event.

The first relied on the pooled cohort equations (PCE), a commonly used risk assessment tool that estimates cardiovascular risk using traditional factors such as age, cholesterol levels, blood pressure, and smoking status.

The second approach measured coronary artery calcium (CAC), which provides a more direct indication of plaque buildup in the arteries supplying the heart.

This measurement uses a computed tomography (CT) scan to detect calcium deposits in the coronary arteries. Calcium can accumulate within atherosclerotic plaque, making it a useful marker of underlying coronary artery disease, even in people who have not developed symptoms.

Unlike traditional risk calculators, which estimate the likelihood of future cardiovascular problems based on personal characteristics and health measurements, calcium scans provide evidence of disease already present in the coronary arteries.

Researchers wanted to determine whether using this information to guide statin recommendations could improve cardiovascular outcomes.

Nearly 5,800 Patients Put Both Methods to the Test

The trial enrolled 5,772 patients from the Canyons and Desert regions of Intermountain Health Care in the United States. Participants had no known history of ASCVD or diabetes and had not previously received statin therapy.

Their average age was 64, and women accounted for 51% of the study population.

Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to one of two groups. One group received statin treatment guidance based on traditional cardiovascular risk scores, while the other received recommendations based on coronary calcium scan results.

Both patients and their physicians were informed of the treatment recommendations generated by the study protocol. However, the final decision about whether to start taking statins remained with the patients and their doctors.

The researchers then tracked major cardiovascular events (MACE; all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and arterial revascularization).

This combined outcome included death from any cause, heart attacks, strokes, and procedures to restore blood flow through narrowed or blocked arteries.

Heart Scans Led to Far Fewer Statin Recommendations

After an average follow-up of 4.2 years, researchers found that major cardiovascular events occurred at exactly the same observed rate in both groups.

A total of 2.7% of patients in each group experienced one of the events included in the study's primary outcome. The estimated relative risk over time was also nearly identical (hazard ratio 0.99; 95% confidence interval 0.71 to 1.38; p=0.045 for noninferiority).

However, this similarity did not establish that the two strategies were equally effective. The study failed to meet its predetermined statistical requirement for demonstrating that the calcium scan approach was not meaningfully worse than conventional risk assessment.

A notable difference emerged in how frequently patients were advised to begin taking statins.

Participants evaluated using traditional risk scores received recommendations to start statin therapy more than three times as often as those whose decisions were guided by coronary calcium measurements.

Despite this substantial difference in treatment recommendations, both groups experienced the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events during the follow-up period.

A Surprising Difference in Statin Adherence

Perhaps the most intriguing finding involved whether patients actually followed their prescribed treatment.

Among those advised to take statins, patients whose recommendations were based on calcium scans were much more likely to adhere to their medication regimen than those assessed using traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

The difference was substantial (62% vs. 23%).

In other words, patients recommended statins based on visible evidence of calcium buildup in their arteries were approximately 2.7 times as likely to follow their medication regimen.

One possible explanation is that seeing evidence of disease in their own arteries makes patients more motivated to take preventive medication. However, the trial did not establish why adherence differed so dramatically between the groups.

The findings raise the possibility that coronary calcium scans could influence not only which patients receive statin recommendations, but also whether those patients consistently take the medications.

What the Findings Mean for Heart Disease Prevention

Despite these potentially important differences, the researchers emphasized that the study could not establish whether calcium scan-guided treatment provides cardiovascular protection comparable to traditional risk assessment.

One important limitation was that fewer participants experienced major cardiovascular events than the investigators had anticipated. With fewer events to analyze, the trial had less statistical power to determine whether a meaningful difference existed between the two approaches.

"The power of the study to detect a difference was reduced by the lower-than-expected event rates and we did not demonstrate noninferiority between the groups," said Doctor Muhlestein, who concluded: "The study did provide important hypothesis-generating insights into the efficiency of statin initiation and adherence when decisions are based on CAC scoring. Taken together, our data could be used to plan an additional well-powered randomized trial comparing CAC with current risk factor-based algorithms."

The findings may help researchers design future trials capable of determining whether coronary calcium scans can improve the efficiency of statin prescribing without compromising cardiovascular protection.

Current European recommendations already recognize a potential role for these measurements. The 2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidemias recommends considering increased coronary calcium scores, when available, as an additional factor in cardiovascular risk assessment.

This guidance applies particularly to people at moderate cardiovascular risk or those whose estimated risk falls near the threshold at which preventive medication would normally be recommended.

For these individuals, evidence of calcium buildup may help doctors make more informed decisions when the need for statin therapy is uncertain.

The CorCal Outcomes findings add to the discussion by suggesting that heart scans may also influence how faithfully patients follow treatment. Whether that advantage translates into better long-term cardiovascular outcomes remains an important question for future research.

#5625. HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: HHS' Chris Klomp on the leap from startups to Medicare

HLTH 2026 Daily Tracker: HHS' Chris Klomp on the leap from startups to Medicare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Fierce Healthcare team is on the ground at HLTH 2026. Stick with this news tracker to catch all the highlights from the show floor, and click here for additional coverage from the conference.

During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason said HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the issue to “remove friction from the patient experience.”

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also says that this information is free to the patient,” she said.

Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.

“The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason said. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”

Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her company looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.

Jain said women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.

“Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain said. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”

To bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain said.

Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.

And, Jain said women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.

“I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain said. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”

Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp said the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.

Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently nominated to serve as Deputy Secretary at HHS and is a rising star in the White House.

He said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.

But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp said.

In addition, he said the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.

"Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he said. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it quickly becomes the most important thing to you."

"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp said.

Houston Methodist announced Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.

Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton, which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.

The vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.

“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find new ways to extend the positive impact,” said Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. #5624. Wegovy Reduces BMI in Kids With Obesity as Young as 6

— Nearly 40% of young children taking the GLP-1 drug dropped below obesity threshold

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. -- Young children ages 6 to 11 years with obesity lost significant weight with the GLP-1 medication semaglutide (Wegovy), according to results from the phase III STEP Young trial.

At week 68, mean body mass index (BMI) decreased by 13.5% with semaglutide compared with an increase of 2.7% with placebo, meeting the trial's primary endpoint (estimated between-group difference -16.2 percentage points, 95% CI -19.4 to -12.9, P<0.001).

By the end of the 104-week treatment period, mean BMI change was -9.4% with semaglutide versus +8.4% with placebo (between-group difference -17.8 percentage points, 95% CI -22.2 to -13.3), reported Ania Jastreboff, MD, PhD, of the Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, Connecticut, and colleagues.

In addition, 38% of participants in the semaglutide group reduced their BMI below the obesity threshold (the 95th percentile for age and sex) by week 68, compared with 2% in the placebo group. At week 104, those rates were 33% and 2%, respectively.

"What we cannot capture with the numbers is the transformation that occurred in these visits. You would walk into the room and the child and their family just felt so different. These children were thriving," Jastreboff said at the ObesityWeek annual meeting.

The findings were simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Semaglutide is approved for adolescents with obesity ages 12 and older, but obesity treatments for younger children are largely restricted to lifestyle modifications, with rare off-label medication use or bariatric surgery. An older daily GLP-1 drug, liraglutide (Saxenda), is approved in the European Union for children ages 6 and older.

"Although lifestyle modifications are a central part of obesity management and support overall health, associated reductions in the BMI are modest (-0.7), with limited evidence for durability," the authors noted, adding that an estimated one in five U.S. children ages 6 to 11 years have obesity. "Thus, the need for more effective treatments is leading to investigation of pharmacotherapeutic options for children."

During a presentation at the meeting, co-author Martin Wabitsch, MD, PhD, of University Medical Center Ulm in Germany, said children with severe obesity have a quality of life "similar to that of children diagnosed with cancer," adding that a 4-year-old with severe obesity has a life expectancy of just 39 years without weight loss.

However, using potent weight-loss medications in prepubertal children carries potential risks, particularly regarding linear growth and lean muscle development. In a subgroup of 50 children assessed via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), semaglutide led to a greater reduction in fat mass percentage and a greater increase in lean soft-tissue percentage than placebo.

Median height gain was lower with semaglutide than placebo at both week 68 (5.7 cm vs 7.8 cm) and week 104 (8.8 cm vs 12.1 cm), accompanied by slower annual height velocity. Bone age, bone mineral density, and pubertal progression (Tanner staging) were similar between groups. Because children with obesity often experience accelerated growth prior to puberty, the researchers suggested the slower height velocity may simply reflect BMI normalization.

Conducted from July 2023 to July 2026 across 48 sites in nine countries, the double-blind STEP Young trial randomized 167 children (2:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (n=112) or placebo (n=55) for 104 weeks, followed by a 7-week off-treatment washout period. All participants received lifestyle counseling.

At least 30% of enrollees were required to have severe obesity (BMI ≥120% of the 95th percentile) or an obesity-related complication such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, or type 2 diabetes. Children with syndromic or hypothalamic obesity, or prior or planned bariatric surgery, were excluded. Maximum weekly doses were capped at 2.4 mg for children weighing more than 132 lb at baseline and 1.7 mg for those weighing 99 to 132 lb.

Participants had a mean age of 10 years; 59% were female, 73% were white, and most were at Tanner stage 1. Mean baseline BMI was 32.4 in the semaglutide group (32.5 in placebo), mean baseline weight was 158.1 lb (159.2 lb in placebo), and just over half had at least one obesity-related complication.

At week 68, secondary cardiometabolic measures, which were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, also favored semaglutide:

In an exploratory analysis, reversion from prediabetes (HbA1c ≥5.7%) to normoglycemia occurred in 93% of semaglutide participants versus 56% of placebo participants at week 68, and in 94% versus 44% at week 104.

"When I am seeing children developing type 2 diabetes at a very young age, this is the type of data that we are really looking for to better understand how these medications can prevent progression," said Daniel Hsia, MD, of Emory University and Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, who was not involved with the study.

As expected with GLP-1 therapies, gastrointestinal issues were the most frequent adverse events. They were mostly mild to moderate, transient, and peaked during the 16-week dose-escalation phase.

Through week 111, rates in the semaglutide versus placebo groups were:

When compared with clinical trial data of semaglutide in adults and adolescents, the proportion of participants who experienced vomiting was lower in STEP Young, Hsia pointed out. "We have to remember that children can have lots of gastroenteritis and other reasons for vomiting, so the high rate of vomiting can be partially explained by that."

Only one child in the semaglutide group discontinued treatment due to gastrointestinal side effects. Serious adverse events -- primarily respiratory or gastrointestinal infections -- occurred in 9% of participants in both groups (10 in the semaglutide group, five in the placebo group). Psychiatric events occurred in 21% of the semaglutide group and 24% of the placebo group. No deaths or new safety signals were reported.

Nearly 40% of children in the placebo arm discontinued injections by week 104, which the authors noted was unsurprising given the lack of weight-loss progress. Other limitations included a predominantly white study population and the absence of baseline screening for eating disorders.

Drugmaker Novo Nordisk has not yet announced plans to submit data from STEP Young to the FDA.

#5623. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

#5619. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

#5618. CBD Didn't Top Placebo for Behavioral Problems in Kids With Intellectual Disability

— Randomized controlled trial adds to evidence of lack of benefit

Cannabidiol (CBD) was no better than placebo for treating severe behavioral problems in kids with intellectual disabilities, a randomized clinical trial in Australia showed.

In an intention-to-treat analysis, patients randomized to CBD had similar behavioral improvement to those who received placebo as measured on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist, Irritability (ABC-I), which captures irritability, aggression, and self-injurious behavior as measured by parent reporting, reported Daryl Efron, MD, of The Royal Children's Hospital in Victoria, Australia, and colleagues.

Over 8 weeks of treatment, ABC-I scores fell from 32.2 to 21.7 in the CBD group and from 30.0 to 19.2 in the placebo group, resulting in a mean difference of 2.4 (95% CI −1.5 to 6.3), they reported in JAMA Pediatrics.

Moreover, rates of adverse events were similar between groups, with 63.1% of those in the CBD group and 60.6% of those in the placebo group experiencing at least one adverse event, the researchers reported.

And there was no advantage for CBD over placebo in any subgroup analysis, including among patients with a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), who accounted for 84% of trial participants.

"The results suggest that CBD should not be used to treat severe behavioral problems in this population," Efron and team wrote.

In an accompanying editorial, Adi Aran, MD, and Dalit Cayam-Rand, MD, both of Shaare Zedek Medical Center in Jerusalem, Israel, noted that the findings were similar to those of a North American multicenter trial conducted among youths ages 6 to 17 years with ASD.

"Together, these findings suggest that the lack of benefit of purified CBD is not confined to youths with intellectual disability but extends to youths with ASD across a broad range of cognitive abilities," they wrote, pointing to an additional two trials of youths with ASD that showed no behavioral benefit for CBD.

Overall, the trials demonstrate "the magnitude of the placebo response even among youths with intellectual disability," which "underscores the need for considerable caution when interpreting apparent benefits of novel treatments based on uncontrolled studies or clinical experience," they wrote.

Finally, Aran and Cayam-Rand noted that "this may not be the end of the story for medical cannabis for youths with neurodevelopmental disorders," as ongoing research is evaluating CBD combined with other parts of the cannabis plant such as terpenes and small amounts of tetrahydrocannabinol.

The parallel design, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial by Efron and colleagues took place from May 11, 2021 to May 8, 2025 across three children's hospitals in Australia. Youths between the ages of 6 and 18 with an intellectual disability and severe behavioral problems were eligible. Intellectual disability was defined as an IQ of less than 70 within 2 years of enrollment and a deficit in adaptive functioning.

In all, 132 patients were randomized 1:1 to either placebo or to 10 mg/kg/d CBD isolate in oil, both taken orally for 8 weeks, and then a 4-week follow-up. Eight patients were either lost to follow up, randomized in error, or had incomplete answers, and 17 discontinued treatment, resulting in 61 patients in the CBD group and 63 in the placebo group.

Three-quarters of patients were male and the mean age was 11.2 years. Most patients were taking a concomitant psychotropic medication at baseline (87%).

Parent-reported scores on the ABC-I subscale assessed at 8 weeks was the primary outcome. Exploratory outcomes included the four remaining subscales of the ABC (social withdrawal, stereotypic behavior, hyperactivity or noncompliance, and inappropriate speech), as well as anxiety, participation in activities, sleep, parenting stress, and parent mental health.

Efron and colleagues noted the study was limited by its heterogenous study sample. Plus, the fixed-dose of 10 mg/kg/d CBD was based on a pediatric epilepsy study, but other research has used smaller doses. While authors believe this dose was adequate to identify a treatment effect, it's also possible that behavioral effects could occur at lower doses, they noted.
