#5600. Inflation, Supply Policies to Have Most Impact on Housing Affordability Post-Elections: Economists

American voters made it clear that affordability was one of the main drivers that tipped them in favor of putting Democrats in control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections.

Democratic candidates flipped both the House of Representatives and Senate blue, buoyed by voters who have seen their everyday living costs skyrocket under the second Trump administration—and made it clear they wanted change.

But now the real work of making those campaign promises a reality begins—with housing affordability a top concern. Any solutions Congress might come up with to combat rising housing costs will take time to put into motion and generally inspire bipartisan cooperation, three top economists tell RISMedia.

Before any policies come into play, economists say inflation is a critical risk to mortgage rate stability and, in turn, the health of the housing market.

Inflation, economic headwinds top issues to watch

Getting inflation under control and expanding housing supply without creating outpaced demand could help shape housing affordability, economists say.

October’s hotter-than-expected inflation reading, up 0.4% instead of the 0.3% forecasted month-over-month, makes it highly likely the Federal Reserve will hike rates when it meets in December. In fact, 90% of analysts polled by CME Group anticipate the Fed will hike its target rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00% to 4.25%.

“What matters most for buyers and sellers is whether inflation eases and mortgage rates become more affordable and the labor market stays healthy,” says Odeta Kushi, deputy chief economist with First American Financial.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Another inflationary metric to watch is the U.S. national debt, Kushi notes, which now stands at more than $40 trillion. This will become even more urgent when the current debt limit of $41.1 trillion is reached by May or mid-2027. If there’s a congressional standoff over increasing the debt limit, that could drive inflation—and borrowing costs—higher while creating more financial market volatility, she explained.

But getting inflation under control depends on a lot of moving parts, according to Jake Krimmel, senior economist with Realtor.com®. Under the Trump administration, it’s impossible to pinpoint those moving parts amid a trade war (and tariffs), geopolitical tensions and mixed economic readings.

Krimmel stressed that inflation also erodes purchasing power. “Inflation eats away at paychecks and makes it harder for people to save.”

“The big wild card heading into 2027 is the same one that we’ve been talking about probably since February, which is the effect of the (Iran) War on the longer end of the curve, the Fed’s rate path and the economy more broadly, especially with respect to inflation, consumer confidence and consumer spending,” Krimmel says. “We don’t know what 2027 will bring, but uncertainty is a feature in this market.”

Mischa Fisher, Zillow’s chief economist, points to a simple formula that will bring mortgage rates down to more palatable levels for homebuyers to act.

“We know, generally speaking, that the best way out of this is higher incomes, lower mortgage rates and more supply,” Fisher says.

According to Zillow’s October housing report, the monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home reached $2,004, up 12.8% from a year ago. That means a median-income household would need to spend 34.7% of its income on total housing costs—up from 32.7% a year ago and far beyond the typical 30% benchmark, Zillow reported.

Fisher noted that the Democrats’ sweep of the midterms hasn’t altered Zillow’s housing forecasts, which call for rates to stay in the 7% range, flat-to-lower sales volume compared to 2026 and home values that rise slightly on paper but decline slightly in real terms after adjusting for inflation.

Could Congress pull any meaningful levers for housing?

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, they’ll have their work cut out for them to deliver for voters who made affordability a central election motivation. However, with President Donald Trump already pledging to use the power of his pen to veto Democrat-led bills, will any meaningful housing legislation see the light of day?

“When we have this period where Congress is controlled by one party and the executive branch is controlled by the other party, typically, that doesn’t foretell close collaboration on policy,” Fisher says. “But I think we have seen that in the case of housing, there is a bipartisan agreement that there’s room to improve the environment. That’s what we’re watching to see play out.”

Fisher notes that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed earlier this year, offers “a real bipartisan blueprint for how policymakers can work together to specifically improve housing.” The timing couldn’t be more crucial as the gap between Americans’ incomes and affordable housing widens.

Kushi adds that Congress should look at policies that make it “easier, cheaper and faster to build and bring more homes to the market.”

While it’s too early to know what lawmakers have in mind to help ease affordability pressures in the housing market, Krimmel cautions that any government stalemates—a shutdown or lapses in government funding—could be disastrous for the 10-year Treasury yield, which directly impacts mortgage rate movements. A government shutdown can also disrupt economic data collection, making it harder to gauge progress on inflation.

“We already have enough pressure on the 10-year,” Krimmel says. “We don’t need anything else.”

All three economists agree that improving housing affordability involves addressing the supply side, among other action items.

The U.S. has an estimated supply gap of 4.03 million homes, according to Realtor.com. Closing the gap, Krimmel says, means boosting new construction, which needs to be “easier to build.” Lawmakers should “encourage states and localities to adopt more permissive local zoning laws and also streamline that permitting process,” Krimmel says, cautioning that it will take time to see any gains.

For now, Realtors® should track local inventory and price trends to help guide their clients more effectively. Fisher notes that affordability-related softness and price pressures will persist in parts of the Mountain West and Sun Belt, while supply-constrained coastal markets where new building isn’t as robust face upward pressure.

Existing-home inventory is still being suppressed by the mortgage lock-in effect, as owners may be reluctant to sell and give up their pandemic-era low rates. More realistic pricing from sellers can help listings go under contract and give buyers more negotiating power. But a more buyer-friendly market doesn’t necessarily mean homes are affordable to more buyers, Krimmel says.

Only time will tell if income growth can keep up with housing costs—and if Congress can act quickly enough to start meaningfully improving affordability to help ease Americans’ financial strain.

Deborah Kearns is a freelance editor and writer with more than 15 years of experience covering real estate, mortgages and personal finance topics. Deborah previously held editorial leadership and writing roles at NerdWallet, Bankrate, LendingTree and RE/MAX World Headquarters.

#5599. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5597. Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. In a study involving more than 120,000 older adults, researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed) found that patients taking certain medications to strengthen their bones were significantly less likely to develop dementia.

The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures. The findings suggest that these established treatments could potentially serve a second purpose by helping protect the aging brain. The research, conducted by scientists in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed's LKS Faculty of Medicine, was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia.

More than 55 million people worldwide currently live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050. The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a major global health priority. Although the first medications designed to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have recently gained approval, their high costs, limited suitability for some patients, and questions about their effectiveness remain important challenges.

These obstacles have increased interest in finding affordable ways to prevent or delay dementia before symptoms develop. One promising approach is to identify existing medications that might offer benefits beyond the conditions they were originally designed to treat.

The Surprising Connection Between Bone Health and Dementia

Osteoporosis and dementia often affect the same older adults. Osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures, while dementia progressively affects memory, thinking, and the ability to carry out everyday activities. The two conditions also share several risk factors, including older age, being female, and low levels of physical activity.

Previous research by the same HKUMed team established that osteoporosis and fractures are independent risk factors for dementia. The researchers also found that people already living with dementia face an increased likelihood of falling and breaking bones.

This relationship raises an intriguing possibility: medications that treat osteoporosis might also help reduce dementia risk.

Among the most commonly prescribed osteoporosis treatments are alendronate and zoledronate, both of which belong to the NBP drug class. These medications work by slowing the breakdown of bone tissue, helping maintain bone strength and reduce the likelihood of fractures.

Scientists have also begun uncovering evidence that some of the biological processes influenced by these drugs may be involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. This overlap has prompted researchers to investigate whether NBPs might provide benefits for the brain as well as the skeleton.

Study of 120,000 Patients Finds Up to 24% Lower Dementia Risk

To explore this possibility, the HKUMed researchers examined electronic medical records from across Hong Kong, analyzing data from more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older. All participants had osteoporosis or fragility fractures, which are breaks that can occur after relatively minor injuries because the bones have become weakened.

The records covered the period from 2005 through 2020, allowing the team to investigate how different osteoporosis treatments were associated with dementia risk over time.

The results revealed a notable difference. Patients taking NBPs had a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared with patients who received no osteoporosis medication.

The association was even stronger when NBP users were compared with patients taking other types of osteoporosis drugs. In that comparison, dementia risk was 24% lower among those receiving NBPs.

Women and patients who had experienced hip fractures appeared to show particularly strong associations between NBP treatment and reduced dementia risk.

The researchers also estimated that treating 48 patients with NBPs over five years could potentially prevent one case of dementia. If future research confirms that the medications directly reduce dementia risk, the implications could be substantial, particularly for older adults who already need treatment for osteoporosis.

Because the findings come from an observational study, they do not establish that the drugs themselves prevent dementia. However, they provide evidence supporting further investigation into whether these medications could help delay or prevent cognitive decline.

Could Existing Osteoporosis Drugs Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Professor Cheung Ching-lung, Associate Professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed, believes the findings highlight the possibility that a familiar osteoporosis treatment could deliver two important health benefits.

"Our study provides evidence that NBPs may offer dual benefits in strengthening bones and reducing fracture risk, as well as potentially preventing ADRD. Their potential neuroprotective role provides an empirical basis and supports future research on the actual effectiveness of this medication in preventing or delaying cognitive decline associated with ADRD."

The potential advantage of this approach is that NBPs are already widely available and have an established history of use in treating osteoporosis. Rather than developing an entirely new medication from scratch, researchers could investigate whether these existing treatments offer additional protection for people at elevated risk of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant as populations around the world grow older and the number of people affected by dementia continues to rise.

"These findings are significant as they demonstrate a potential approach for reducing dementia risk in a vulnerable population using safe and widely available NBPs. In our rapidly aging society, these findings suggest that while waiting for the novel therapies, existing medications can also provide additional protection for high-risk populations," said Professor Cheung.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether NBPs can directly prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Nevertheless, the results suggest that medications already prescribed to protect aging bones may also have an important role to play in protecting brain health.

The research was led by Professor Cheung Ching-lung of the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed. Dr Sing Chor-wing, from the same department, served as the study's first author.

Additional researchers included Professor Chan Koon-ho, Dr Patrick Chiu Ka-chun, and Professor Kathryn Tan Choon-beng, all from the Department of Medicine in the School of Clinical Medicine at HKUMed.

Materials provided by The University of Hong Kong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5595. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

#5594. NIH’s infectious disease unit has a new head at last

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Good morning and happy Tuesday! Today’s newsletter includes good news for international students, bad news for the makers of signs proclaiming “zero tolerance” for violence in hospitals, and mixed news for children with rare brain disorders. Read on!

No branch of the NIH has faced more scrutiny than the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. For nearly four decades, the institute was run by Anthony Fauci; it’s since become a major focus of Republicans looking to re-litigate the Covid pandemic.

The institute has been without a permanent director since Jeanne Marrazzo was forced out in 2025 for objecting to grant terminations. Now officials have announced that acting director John Powers III will take the lead role.

Powers is a physician-scientist who’s worked at NIAID in several clinical research positions. He has run the institute in an acting capacity since June. Earlier this year, he co-authored a paper with NIH director Jay Bhattacharya that argued NIAID should move away from its focus on HIV and pandemic preparedness, instead prioritizing broader categories of infectious disease and immunology.

Read more from STAT’s Anil Oza, including Powers’ response to questions about health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s position on vaccines.

One of the key tenets of Alcoholics Anonymous is surrender to a higher power. There, and in other organizations, faith-based addiction recovery can serve an important role in supporting people trying to stay sober.

But experts warn the Trump administration’s full-throated embrace of these programs will result in federal grants to centers that don’t always provide evidence-based treatment. As STAT’s Theresa Gaffney explains, some faith-based addiction centers don’t allow participants to use drugs like methadone, which is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for opioid use disorder.

Kennedy also has expressed support for unconventional (and scientifically dubious) approaches to treatment, including “wellness farms,” where people reside in nature and engage in manual labor. Read more about the tricky balance experts hope Kennedy can strike.

That’s the share of women who provided care to a friend or family member with a health problem in the past 30 days, according to a new analysis of 2025 data from the National Center for Health Statistics. Women were about 32% more likely than men to have provided care, offering a real world data point to back up the viral Saturday Night Live sketch about the gendered dynamics of caregiving (which makes it sound much less funny than it is! Give a watch here).

Last year, researchers thought they’d had a breakthrough — they finally engineered a virus to ferry gene therapy to the brain. Experts were hopeful this innovation could cure Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and slew of rare diseases.

Then the first person to undergo treatment with this new technique — a 3 year old — died of brain swelling 65 hours later, sending fear and uncertainty through the industry. Nearly a year later, researchers have unveiled how the process can be shored up for the future, with ideas for new tests and trials to ensure safety. Read more here.

A proposal by the Trump administration to cap the amount of time foreign students and scholars can spend in the country has been struck down in court. In a decision Monday, a federal judge said the rule was “arbitrary” and “capricious,” writing that the government did not sufficiently consider the ramifications of the new policy.

In his story on the ruling, Anil Oza breaks down why this matters: “International researchers make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates and around 60% of postdoctoral researchers. About 40% of American Nobel laureates in the sciences are immigrants.” Read more.

Violence against doctors and nurses has jumped in recent years, due to an ugly swirl of understaffing, overcrowding, and pandemic-era stress that hasn’t quite faded. In response, many hospitals have started to hang signs declaring “zero tolerance” for violence or other bad behavior from patients.

The problem, according to three professors, is that these signs don’t actually help protect workers. Instead, they signal to families that care is something that can be withheld. The signs often include long lists about things that patients shouldn’t do, without a similar standards for nurses and doctors.

“The content of the signs sends clear messages to patients and families about their tenuous status and value in the institution,” they write. Read more.

#5593. The ‘Andy Warhol of Real Estate’ Unveils a $2.9M Portland Home Shaped Like a ‘Bouquet of Flowers’

After much anticipation, internationally acclaimed architect Robert Oshatz has unveiled his latest architectural tour de force, a jaw-dropping, ultra-modern residence in Portland’s West Hills neighborhood.

Listed for $2,888,000, the newly completed home was designed by Oshatz, an apprentice of Frank Lloyd Wright Jr. It is one of five planned homes tucked into the forest, four of which have yet to be built.

“It took about three years, but it is finally complete,” said listing agent Terry Sprague of LUXE | Forbes Global Properties. “Robert Oshatz is like the Andy Warhol/Peter Max of real estate. His designs are so completely unusual compared to commoditized architecture.”

The four-bedroom home’s steel-framed structure has curved wood ceilings, circular windows, disappearing glass walls, and an elevator that provides easy access to all four levels.

“It’s an incredibly visual home that’s designed for a collector who enjoys its shape and architecture,” Sprague noted. “I think the next buyer will be very compelled by the opportunity to own an appreciating piece of real estate.”

The architect used unique shapes, windows, and design to let light dance through the 3,700-square-foot space at various times during the day.

“He built in prisms,” Sprague said. “There’s a piece of glass set in a certain way that you see rainbows throughout the home. Every wall is a sculpture. Every window is a sculpture.”

“This is a wooded-view property,” he added. “It’s like living in nature and feels like a modern treehouse as the home is cantilevered out to the view.”

Sprague believes the residence will likely be used as a second or third home.

“Baby boomers are our largest consumer right now,” he said. “They’re high-net worth people from states like Arizona and Florida where they live full-time, and are buying very expensive pied-a-tierres like this.”

One of the biggest luxuries of living in nature is being able to wake up somewhere beautiful, Sprague said.

“Portland and the Pacific Northwest are one of the most beautiful places in the world with its Columbian Gorge, high mountain deserts, and clean air,” he noted. “This is a one-of-a-kind piece of architecture that has a whole different meaning than most real estate.”

There are four more lots that are "build ready" and seeking a “very creative, understanding curator.”

When complete, the five “one-of-a-kind” homes will share 90,000 square feet of forested acreage. Oshatz is locally known for his organic designs, including the Wilkinson Residence, the Rosenthal Residence, and the Fennell Residence.

“He had a vision for the homes to resemble a bouquet of flowers, so he hired Todd Delahunt as the general contractor to build this home,” Sprague added. “Robert Oshatz is over 80 years old and wanted to complete this home. Hopefully, this might inspire other custom builds, or the lots could be sold off to the buyer of this home.”

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a new breast cancer drug from Roche, teeing up the launch of a medicine that the company has said could become its top-selling product ever, STAT says. The approval for the drug, known as giredestrant, was one of the most important regulatory decisions Roche had been awaiting. It gives the company another foothold in breast cancer treatments, a field in which it has a storied history with the drug Herceptin through its Genentech subsidiary, though in recent years it has fallen behind rivals in oncology. Analysts broadly see giredestrant becoming a multibillion-dollar blockbuster if Roche wins approval in other forms of breast cancer.

New results from a closely watched clinical trial showed that weight loss drugs are effective for children as young as 6, though some doctors say they are concerned about the prospect of prescribing these medications to such young patients, The New York Times writes. The study, presented at the medical conference Obesity Week, examined children ages 6 to 11 who were taking semaglutide, the compound in Ozempic and Wegovy. Most children in the trial had severe obesity, meaning they had a body mass index of 35 or higher. After 68 weeks, nearly 40% of those who took the drug no longer had obesity, compared with none of the patients on a placebo.

#5591. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

"Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," said corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," said Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

This extended timeline was especially important because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves."

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

#5589. How Training Veterans in Skilled Trades Could Speed Up Homebuilding and Ease Housing Costs

A severe shortage of skilled workers entering the residential construction sector has had a major impact on affordability, but the Home Builders Institute (HBI) believes the country’s large veteran population may be part of the solution.

The skilled labor shortage has led to an increase in construction time, with each home taking nearly two months longer to build, according to an HBI study. Due to the delays, there was a reduction of 19,000 homes built in 2024, representing an economic loss of over $8 billion, the study found.

Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimated that the construction industry needs to attract roughly 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 new workers in 2027 to meet demand for construction services.

There are a number of factors in the past 30 years that have led to the labor shortage, according to HBI CEO Ed Brady. First, a strong push for four-year degrees led many young people toward academic careers rather than trades. With more people retiring from the workforce than entering, the shortage began.

The issue was compounded during the financial crisis of 2008, when the residential construction field lost tons of skilled workers because there wasn’t enough work. Without enough housing construction, workers left for jobs in manufacturing and hospitality or retired early, according to Brady.

More recently, rocky immigration policies have challenged the skilled labor workforce, Brady explains.

When finding a solution to the shortage became dire, HBI believed that the veteran and transitioning military population was “an untapped market.” The result was the HBI Military Services Program, which trains veterans, transitioning military service members, and their dependents in skilled trades.

On Monday, HBI and Invitation Homes announced a new partnership that will continue HBI’s mission to create opportunities for transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families.

The partnership includes an unspecified investment from Invitation Homes in HBI’s Military Services Program. It will also open doors for former military service members who complete HBI training to access job opportunities with the premier leasing and management company.

For nearly a decade, HBI has been raising awareness of the benefits of a career in a skilled trade among former members. It has proceeded to train, certify, and assist veterans and their families in finding successful careers.

HBI’s Military Services Program was supported early on by major companies like The Home Depot Foundation and Dewalt. It was recently given a $1 million gift from Google.org, and now Invitation Homes has joined the worthy cause.

These vital investments help HBI reach even more service members on their mission, according to Brady.

“It provides scale. We’re not changing our model—we feel like our model works. We introduce them to the industry, we train them in the industry, we certify them, we connect them to the industry to get a job,” Brady tells Realtor.com®.

“But the dollars from Invitation Homes, the dollars that Google have given us to apply into the veteran space just gives us more scale. We can provide better service, and we can grow our programs to serve more veterans, more transitioning military, even the spouses of veterans.”

Expanding training programs for former military could make a huge difference in the skilled labor shortage being experienced by residential construction.

“In many cases, the demographic of soldiers that want to be outside, want to work with their hands, and have that physicality, it’s natural for them to look at our industry,” says Brady. “They’ve got more discipline, they know how to create a task and how to do a job. They have a desire to be productive and build a career.”

Brady has also observed that many veterans want to “control their own destiny” once they leave the military. The desire to not be dependent on anyone else or an organization makes them great candidates for entrepreneurship, business ownership, and contracting roles.

For Philip Shealy, HBI offered a path when he was unsure of next steps.

After spending five years as an Army infantryman at Fort Drum in New York and Fort Stewart in Georgia, he had no clue what he wanted to do next, Shealy recalls. He decided to take advantage of the DoD SkillBridge to learn some skills before departing the service.

“I saw the HBI program and thought, even if I don’t go into the skilled trades like that, that will be information I hold for the rest of my life. It’ll be great for owning a home or just knowing a thing here or there,” Shealy tells Realtor.com.

“But the program does a pretty cool thing where they bring in recruiters from local companies. And they brought one in that sounded like something I wanted to do. So I applied with him and ended up getting the job.”

Shealy now works for Ace Electric, an electrical contractor in southern Georgia, alongside several fellow veterans who went through the same HBI program.

The three-month program was conducted right at Fort Stewart. Participants learned everything they needed to enter a career in carpentry or electrical work, and they even built little homes on base as part of the training.

Shealy recalls one of the instructors being former military himself, so he was able to communicate effectively by building upon military skills and terminology and translating them to trade terms.

Many skills emphasized by the military, such as leadership and the ability to take instruction and corrections well, have transferred well to his career in a skilled trade.

Shealy shares HBI’s belief that trade jobs and the military attract the same type of person, making it a logical next step for many leaving the service.

“People that like to work with their hands, many of which are going to be hard workers and aren’t going to stop until the job gets done and done well—I think a lot of it transfers well over,” says Shealy.

For those still considering next steps, he says to give the SkillBridge and HBI programs a shot, because you may just end up finding a great path.

“When we’re getting out, it can be a very scary thing, not knowing where you’re going to end up,” says Shealy. “From my personal experience going through HBI programming, I had no clue what I wanted to do, and then I ended up finding something I’ll enjoy doing for a long time.”

Brady also emphasizes the longevity of a trade career.

“This is a career path, not just a job. Getting into the trades is something that you can hang your hat on for your career,” says Brady. “And it’s not a career that’s going to be diminished by technology or AI. Certainly innovation will make it more efficient, but you’re not going to take away roofers. You’re not going to take away plumbers.”

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

#5587. Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke

New preliminary research involving more than 440,000 American adults has uncovered a concerning association between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. The findings suggest that even occasional marijuana use may be linked to higher odds of cardiovascular problems, raising new questions about the health effects of a substance that is becoming increasingly common across the United States.

The research, presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, found that the association was not limited to people who frequently used cannabis. It also appeared across different methods of consumption (smoked or edible, etc.). Researchers emphasized that cannabis use should be considered when discussing heart health and stroke prevention.

Scientific Sessions 2026 took place November 6 through 9 in Chicago, bringing together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, clinical advances, and emerging evidence.

Cannabis refers to the plant itself, while marijuana is a commonly used term for cannabis products containing enough THC to produce psychoactive effects.

Marijuana Use Is Rising Across the United States

"Previous research has indicated that cannabis use is rapidly increasing in the United States, with 1 in 6 adults in 2024 reporting having used it within the last month, up from 1 in 10 in 2020 -- a 51% increase," said study author Aabha Divya, M.B.B.S., M.Ch., an assistant professor in the division of cardiothoracic surgery at the Tulane University School of Medicine in New Orleans.

Earlier research conducted between 2016 and 2020 had already identified associations between cannabis consumption and unfavorable cardiovascular outcomes. Those findings also suggested that using cannabis more frequently during a given month was connected to greater cardiovascular risk.

However, the evidence has not always been consistent. With recreational marijuana becoming legal in more places and cannabis products increasingly available, Divya and colleagues wanted to investigate these possible health effects in a larger population.

"We wanted to expand on this earlier work because cannabis use has become increasingly common in the United States, as recreational legalization and commercial availability of various products with cannabis have also expanded. Previous studies have raised concerns about possible cardiovascular effects; however, the results have not been consistent," Divya said.

The researchers examined information collected through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a large telephone survey of American adults. They combined responses from jurisdictions that collected information about cannabis consumption between 2020 and 2024.

Participants answered questions about their marijuana use and whether a healthcare professional had ever diagnosed them with cardiovascular conditions, including a heart attack, stroke, or coronary heart disease.

Even Occasional Marijuana Use Was Linked to Higher Stroke Odds

One of the most striking findings was that infrequent cannabis use was associated with cardiovascular problems. In fact, the researchers did not find the steady increase in cardiovascular risk with more frequent use that they had expected.

The analysis revealed several important associations:

These findings were unexpected because the relationship between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease did not consistently become stronger as consumption increased.

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward. We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease," Divya said.

Although the study cannot establish that marijuana directly causes strokes or other cardiovascular conditions, the findings suggest that occasional consumption should not automatically be considered free of potential cardiovascular concerns.

"As cannabis use becomes more common, it is increasingly important that people and their healthcare professionals include it in conversations about cardiovascular health, just as they discuss tobacco, alcohol and other commonly used substances," she added.

Experts Urge Greater Attention to Cannabis and Heart Health

Robert L. Page II, Pharm.D., M.S.P.H., FAHA, who led the writing group responsible for the American Heart Association's 2020 cannabis scientific statement, said the findings add to growing concerns about marijuana's possible cardiovascular effects.

One challenge in evaluating those effects is that many cannabis users also smoke tobacco. Because tobacco is already an established cardiovascular risk factor, separating its effects from those of cannabis can be difficult.

Page, who was not involved in the research, explained why the new findings deserve attention.

"Unfortunately, many patients who use cannabis may also smoke tobacco, which completely clouds the issue when addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk. In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case. This is the second observational study to suggest that cannabis exposure (without tobacco smoking) may be a potential risk factor for developing cardiovascular disease. Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events. To this end, clinicians should be addressing cannabis use with their patients as they would tobacco use when considering the risk of cardiovascular disease."

Page is a professor in the department of clinical pharmacy and the department of physical medicine/rehabilitation at the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences in Aurora, Colorado.

How Researchers Studied Nearly Half a Million Americans

The analysis included 442,906 adults living in the United States (average age of 49 years; approximately half women). Their responses came from telephone surveys conducted through the BRFSS.

Researchers used survey information collected from 2020 through 2024, focusing on states that had included an optional marijuana questionnaire. Between 16 and 24 states participated in this portion of the survey each year, meaning the analysis did not represent every state.

Participants reported how many days they had consumed cannabis during the preceding month. The questions covered multiple ways of using marijuana (smoking, vaping or ingesting gummies or other cannabis-containing foods).

The researchers divided participants into four categories based on their reported use:

Participants also indicated whether they had ever received a diagnosis of heart attack, heart disease, heart-related chest pain, or stroke.

To better distinguish the association with cannabis from other potential explanations, the researchers accounted for numerous established cardiovascular risk factors. These included demographic characteristics, tobacco smoking, alcohol consumption, obesity, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, physical inactivity, education, and income.

Why the Findings Do Not Prove Marijuana Causes Strokes

Despite the large number of participants, the study has several limitations that affect how its findings should be interpreted.

First, the analysis examined associations between reported cannabis use and previously diagnosed cardiovascular conditions at a single point in time. This means researchers could not determine whether marijuana use preceded the cardiovascular problems or whether it directly contributed to them.

The information also depended on participants accurately recalling and reporting their cannabis consumption and medical histories (making them subject to potential errors in memory). Such reports may not always reflect actual patterns of use or diagnoses.

Another limitation was the lack of information about the strength of the cannabis products participants consumed or the quantities they used. Without those details, the researchers could not evaluate whether THC potency or the amount consumed influenced the observed associations.

The researchers also acknowledged that some participants may have reduced or discontinued cannabis consumption after being diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. As a result, the group reporting no cannabis use in the previous month may have included former users.

These uncertainties make it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how consumption frequency affects cardiovascular health. Nevertheless, the findings add to growing evidence that cannabis use deserves closer examination as a possible factor in heart disease and stroke.

As marijuana becomes more widely available and its use continues to increase, researchers and healthcare professionals are emphasizing the importance of discussing cannabis alongside other substances that may affect cardiovascular health.

#5584. Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health

The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

"These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products."

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events

To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

"Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

"This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events."

Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

#5583. America’s Trillion-Dollar Credit Card Debt Threatens To Lock Millions Out of the Housing Market

With prices still alarmingly high, it comes as no surprise that Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards more than ever.

But doing so could be silently sabotaging any hope of owning a home, if you’re not careful.

Last week, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York published its latest household debt report.

Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier, and total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans, and student loans, expanded by $334 billion for the period to a record $19.1 trillion.

High levels of debt are problematic for anyone, but most especially for first-time homebuyers. If your ambitions for 2027 include buying a home, it’s important to get your debt in check before it’s too late.

According to TransUnion’s most recent quarterly credit industry insights report, the number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million up from 174.8 million.

The ease of use means most people turn to credit cards for their everyday purchases, like groceries, gas, and utility bills—all of which have seen a steep increase in prices over the past two years.

Now, if you’re someone who pays off their credit card in full each month, you’re in the clear. If not, the average interest rate on a new credit card offer currently stands at about 24%, and debt can accumulate quickly.

And this can cause an array of issues for first-time homebuyers.

"Issues arising from high levels of consumer debt are amplified for first-time homebuyers as they typically have less savings, limited financial history, and tighter financial conditions,” John Donikian, vice president of Best Interest Financial in West Bloomfield, MI, tells Realtor.com®.

Firstly, carrying too much debt can negatively affect your credit score, a vital metric in getting a mortgage.

While there is no firm number to qualify for a mortgage, a good credit score ranges from 700 to 749, and most conventional loans typically require at least 620. Lenders may accept lower scores if you have a larger down payment or other strong financial factors.

The higher your balances are, the more your score is dragged down, which can not only affect the interest rate a lender can offer you, but also keep you from getting a mortgage with some lenders entirely.

“Your credit score doesn’t just determine if you are approved; it influences your interest rate and the monthly payment you are offered,” says Jake Vehige, president of mortgage lending at Neighbors Bank.

“Even a small difference in interest rates can add up to thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.”

Secondly, as part of the process of getting a mortgage, lenders will look at your debt-to-income ratio to see how much house you can afford.

If a lender looks at your total monthly debt payments against your gross monthly income and your DTI exceeds its caps, your application could be delayed or even denied outright.

But both of those instances can be reversed, with time and a fixed budget that allows you to pay off your debt. In other words, your credit score can rebound.

Where first-time buyers are really at a disadvantage by accumulating so much credit card debt is the drain it will put on their savings.

The money that you’ll need to rack up to pay off the 20%-plus interest on your bills could have been money saved for your down payment, closing costs, and repair funds.

Many lenders also require proof of postclosing cash reserves, which is much harder to build while paying down high-interest debt.

“Ideally, you want to keep your credit card balances at no more than 20% to 30% of your maximum credit limit," explains Jeremy Schachter, branch manager at Fairway Independent Mortgage Corp. in Phoenix.

"For example, if you have a $1,000 limit, don’t go over a balance higher than $200 to $300. Anything that exceeds that amount can lower your credit score and make it difficult to get approved for a mortgage with a good rate.”

Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. She previously served as the managing editor at HollywoodLife.com, the executive editor at PerezHilton.com, and as a managing editor at Mediavine. Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.

#5582. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

The type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

The findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of new bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

"What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," said Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

More conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

"The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming new bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

This is especially important for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a new activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

The findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.
