#5581. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5580. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline

To investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

"This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect."

This effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

"I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed."

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

The research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," said Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

This increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well."

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

The researchers then plan to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce important features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#5579. Mapped: Where the Most Homeowners Own Their Homes Outright With No Mortgage

Roughly 3 in 5 American homeowners pay a mortgage every month, yet the share of those who own their property outright is steadily growing—with at least half of all homeowners in three states now completely mortgage-free.

According to a new Realtor.com® data analysis of the recently released 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, 59% of homeowners carried a mortgage last year, while 41% owned their homes free and clear.

That marks a major shift from 2010, when fewer than a third of homes (32.8%) were owned outright while 67% carried home loan debt.

Mortgaged homeownership has shrunk across all four regions, though reliance on financing still varies significantly by geography. The West had the highest mortgage debt rate at 63.8%, while the South recorded the lowest at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest tied at 58.7%.

At the state level, West Virginia led the nation with 56.6% of its homeowners living mortgage-free, followed by Mississippi (52.7%) and New Mexico (50%).

On the other side of the spectrum, Washington, DC, in 2025 logged the lowest share of outright homeownership, at just 26.5%, trailed by Maryland (30.6%) and Colorado (31.6%).

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu explains that the balance between mortgaged and free-and-clear homes meaningfully shapes housing market dynamics, especially at a time when mortgage rates are high.

"Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs," says Xu. "Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs."

Ultimately, those market forces sway inventory levels, home prices, and whether first-time buyers can access homeownership.

With mortgage rates stuck above 7% and the Federal Reserve all but certain to raise interest rates in December—and possibly again in January 2027—to combat inflation, the lock-in effect is poised to chill the market again.

Homeowners sitting on low mortgage rates are reluctant to give them up, keeping much-needed inventory off the market. That supply squeeze, in turn, puts upward pressure on prices and makes it harder for renters to access homeownership.

Free-and-clear owners, however, are not bound by borrowing costs and can list whenever they choose.

"A mortgage-free owner isn’t watching interest rates to decide when to move," Christie Goldman, a real estate agent with Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Central in Charleston, WV, tells Realtor.com. "They can buy their next home with cash, which makes their offer stronger, and they can close on their own timeline without a lender, an appraisal contingency, or rate risk."

Across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, West Virginia stands out with the lowest share of mortgaged homes, at 43.4%, and conversely the highest share of outright ownership, at 56.6%.

Two main forces drive this dynamic: relatively low median home prices and an older population that tends to hold on to properties longer than residents in many other states.

"In West Virginia, a paid-off home isn’t a someday goal. It's how people here live," says Goldman. "When people put down roots here, they stay."

It is common for a local family to purchase a home, raise their children there, and pay it off, often with the next generation buying property in the same community.

According to Goldman, affordability is what makes that cycle possible.

In October 2026, the median asking price in West Virginia was $259,999, well below the national median of $415,000.

"At those prices, owning your home free and clear is a realistic goal here, not a distant dream," says the agent, pointing to the 2025 United Van Lines’ national study that ranked West Virginia as the second-leading inbound destination for movers.

"Many of those buyers sell a higher-priced home elsewhere and can pay cash here," says Goldman. "Once they discover the mountains, the community, and the pace of life, they don’t want to leave."

Xu also attributes West Virginia's high share of mortgage-free owners to the state's slow population growth, particularly among young adults, which has kept new borrowers from entering the market in large numbers.

Between 2015 and 2025, the population aged 18–34 fell 5% in West Virginia, while the same age group in the U.S. grew 3.8%.

Owning one's home outright offers many perks, sharply reducing monthly expenses and creating a buffer against economic headwinds.

"Mortgage-free homeowners have more financial flexibility, especially with today's higher interest rates and rising living costs," Thomas O’Shaughnessy, vice president and real estate broker at Clever Real Estate, tells Realtor.com. "They don't have monthly mortgage payments, which makes it easier to manage expenses, save money, and handle unexpected repairs or emergencies."

In theory, a high percentage of debt-free homeowners can also help unlock inventory for the next wave of buyers.

"They may be more willing to list, downsize, move elsewhere, or buy again," says O'Shaughnessy. "All of these can improve inventory and help move the market in your community."

In West Virginia, however, Goldman notes that high levels of mortgage-free ownership does not necessarily flood the market with fresh listings because people put down deep roots and tend to stay in their homes for decades.

On the flip side, Washington, DC, and Maryland log the highest shares of mortgaged homes in the nation, at 73.5% and 69%, respectively—a trend Xu links to the region's job market.

"Federal, professional, and contracting employment draws midcareer workers, who buy homes and borrow soon after arriving," she notes.

In 2025, nearly 45% of DC homeowners and 36% of Maryland homeowners were aged 35 to 54. Elevated housing costs also force many buyers to finance: The median listing price in DC was $549,000 and $424,894 in Maryland last month.

Given that local homeowners carry so much mortgage debt, rate hikes hit markets like DC and Maryland particularly hard.

"Many buyers there need loans, so fewer can afford to buy, and homeowners with low-rate mortgages are less likely to sell," says Xu.

The latest ACS data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows that in 2025, homeownership among households aged 75 and up rose to 78.3%, up from 75.7% in 2010.

During the same period, the mortgage-free share among this demographic fell from 79.7% to 71.3%. In other words, most baby boomers still own outright, but the share with a loan rose from 20.3% to 28.7%.

Xu says the two trends—more seniors owning their homes, and more of those owners carrying a mortgage—together shape when senior sellers are likely to list.

"A senior with a low-rate loan faces a lock-in effect in today’s high-rate environment," says Xu. "Selling means giving up that cheap financing for a more expensive loan on the next home, which can keep the house off the market longer and slow the handoff to the next generation."

Meanwhile, seniors who own outright can sell on their own schedule, whether for health, care, or downsizing, so their home is more likely to pass to the next generation when the owner’s circumstances change.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5578. Contractor at Site of Brooklyn Building Collapse Was Previously Sued for Negligence

The general contractor overseeing the construction site adjacent to a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn, NY, was previously accused in a lawsuit of compromising the structural integrity of nearby properties during an excavation project, court records show.

Signage at the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., as well as planning documents filed with the Department of Buildings, show that Townhouse Builders, Inc, doing business as Promont, was the general contractor overseeing the construction project.

Building records show that the project involved excavation work directly adjacent to the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. that fully collapsed on Wednesday, killing eight people, including two children, and leaving 18 others injured.

The construction project had a documented history of safety concerns flagged by DOB inspectors, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani says there will be a full investigation into whether any issues at the Bedford Ave. construction site contributed to the collapse.

"If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them accountable," the mayor said.

Now, court records reviewed by Realtor.com® show that Townhouse Builders was accused in a 2020 lawsuit of causing "a breached wall, substantial shifting, settlement and cracking" to an adjacent property during a separate construction job.

New York state records list Mordachai Waisbrod as the CEO of Townhouse Builders. The company and an attorney listed as representing the Townhouse in the 2020 lawsuit did not respond to requests for comment from Realtor.com.

Townhouse Builders has worked on numerous projects across New York, including a retail location on Atlantic Ave., a residential tower on Delancey St. in the Lower East Side, and the redevelopment of a residential tower on Park Row.

In 2016, Townhouse Builders was hired by developer Moris Yeroshalm to serve as general contractors on the construction of a six-story hotel at 1200 Broadway in Brooklyn's Bed-Stuy neighborhood.

In a lawsuit filed in Kings County Supreme Court in 2020, Yeroshalmi alleged that "the construction activity performed by Townhouse at the Project caused damage and compromised the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

The suit alleges that "the construction caused, among other things, a breached wall, substantial shifting, settlement and cracking of Plaintiff's property and the adjacent properties, in addition to broken footing of the adjacent properties and structural destabilization of Plaintiff's property and the adjacent properties."

The suit lists the allegedly damaged properties as 1196 Broadway, and 15 and 17 Patchen Avenue, all located in Brooklyn.

The lawsuit further alleges that 1196 Broadway "was severely damaged by the excavation activity" and that 15 and 17 Patchen Ave. "were severely damaged by the pile driving activities."

In the suit, Yeroshalmi alleges Townhouse "breached their duty and were negligent … by allowing construction activities to compromise and destroy the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

Further, the lawsuit accuses Townhouse of "failing to perform a physical inspection and prepare a proper pre-construction survey of Plaintiff's property prior to performing excavation and underpinning, failing to support the premises walls and by allowing the excavation and underpinning to compromise the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

Yeroshalmi sued for damages totaling more than $1.1 million. The suit remains open with the next hearing in the case to be held in January 2027.

A review of Department of Buildings complaints and violations related to 1200 Broadway show that Townhouse Builders received a Class 2 or "major" violation in 2016 for "failure to monitor adjoining structures for movement in all directions during excavation-related activity that may adversely affect adjoining structures."

That same year, it received a Class 1 violation for "failure to safeguard all persons and property affected by construction operations," noting that the excavator's bucket damaged the brick foundation wall of an adjoining building during excavation. Class 1 violations are "Immediately Hazardous violations" that "must be corrected immediately."

In 2017, it received another Class 2 violation for failure to monitor cracks on adjacent buildings during excavation.

In total, the DOB fined Townhouse Builders $10,400 for those three violations.

Court records show Townhouse Builders, under their own name and Promont, have been sued 67 times since 2012. Thirteen of those cases, including the one mentioned above, remain open. It appears the bulk of those cases have to do with injuries on job sites.

On Wednesday, the Brooklyn district attorney's office announced it was opening a criminal investigation into the cause of the collapse.

“We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy,” District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said in the statement.

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani announced the city would be sweeping 100 other sites associated with five "entities" involved in a construction project adjacent to the collapsed building. The city has since expanded that search to 160 properties. Mamdani and Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani declined to name the five companies they would be focusing their investigation on.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5577. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5576. Canopy Realtor® Association Names Rob Nanfelt Next CEO

Canopy Realtor® Association has announced the appointment of Rob Nanfelt as its next Chief Executive Officer, effective Jan. 4, 2027. Nanfelt succeeds current CEO Anne Marie DeCatsye, who is retiring from the position at the end of 2026 following 26 years of leadership. Nanfelt will also serve as CEO of Canopy Housing Foundation.

As CEO, Canopy noted that Nanfelt will provide strategic and executive leadership to Canopy Realtor® Association and Canopy Housing Foundation, working with their respective Boards to advance their missions, strengthen member value, expand community partnerships, and identify opportunities for innovation and organizational growth. The Canopy Housing Foundation will continue to have a dedicated Executive Director responsible for its programs and activities.

“Our region is strategically poised to grow our economic health within all real estate disciplines,” said Nanfelt. “By reinforcing the vital role government advocacy plays in supporting our industry, we can find solutions to critical issues and advance the real estate profession with a shared purpose. I look forward to galvanizing those strategic goals across the entire breadth of leadership here at Canopy.”

Nanfelt’s 25 years of experience spans the disciplines of executive leadership, association management, strategic planning, government affairs, and public policy, as noted in a release.

In his previous position as Executive Director of the Real Estate & Building Industry Coalition (REBIC), Nanfelt worked with business executives, elected officials, and community leaders to address issues central to the Charlotte region’s economic vitality and long-term growth. Prior to this, he served as Executive Vice President and Government Affairs Director of the Colorado Association of Home Builders, forging new strategic initiatives and becoming a leader in innovation and policy advancement for the industry. Earlier in his career, Nanfelt held several positions on Capitol Hill, including Chief of Staff to U.S. Congressman Bob Schaffer of Colorado.

“My hope was that the search committee would not simply find a successor, but secure someone with the vision, and experience needed to take Canopy to the next level.” said DeCatsye. “I have tremendous confidence in his leadership, fresh perspective, established relationships, and his deep understanding of what it takes to leverage the opportunities ahead. I could not be more excited about Canopy’s future, and I’m thrilled with the selection of Rob Nanfelt as our next CEO.”

Joan Goode, 2026 President of Canopy Realtor® Association, echoed DeCatsye’s sentiment, adding that Nanfelt’s appointment “reflects the Search Committee’s commitment to identifying a proven executive with the experience, relationships, and vision to lead Canopy into the future.”

“He is exceptionally well positioned to strengthen Canopy’s influence, advance its mission, support the success of our members, and build upon its respected legacy,” she continued.

Canopy noted that Nanfelt’s appointment represents an important milestone in its planned leadership transition. Beginning in 2027, Canopy Realtor® Association and Canopy MLS will operate under separate executive leadership and governance structures, allowing each organization to focus on its distinct mission while maintaining collaboration through shared leadership and administrative services. Steve Byrd, who became CEO of Canopy MLS in August 2026, will continue in that role.

For DeCatsye, the transition carries a personal connection.

“Before joining Canopy 26 years ago, I spent six years as Deputy Executive Director of REBIC, an experience that gave me a deep appreciation for advocacy and how it moves our industry forward,” she shared. “There is something wonderfully fitting about Rob following a similar path and I am delighted that he will lead with those ideals fully embedded in his mission for Canopy.”

For more information, visit https://www.canopyrealtors.com/.

#5575. Presley Gerber’s Hollywood Hills Home Hits the Market for $3.6 Million—Nearly 2 Months After His Death

Presley Gerber’s Hollywood Hills home has hit the market for $3.59 million, less than two months after the model’s death at age 27.

The son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, who passed away on Sept. 20, snapped up the property for $3.4 million in March 2023.

Now, nearly two months after his tragic death, the property has hit the market for $3.6 million with real estate agent Cindy Ambuehl of Christie's AKG, as first reported by TMZ.

The dwelling is described as "beautifully reimagined mid-century architecture meets modern luxury in the heart of the Hollywood Hills."

The home features four bedrooms, three bathrooms, and sprawls across 3,000 square feet.

Built in 1955, the home sits behind gates in the Hollywood Hills. Canyon views frame the property, while the living spaces connect to outdoor areas through large sliding glass doors.

Inside, the main gathering space combines wood floors and a fireplace with access to the kitchen and dining areas.

The primary suite and guest bedrooms also open onto the pool and patio, allowing residents to step outside directly from their rooms.

The guest accommodation is attached to the house, according to the listing. It contains one bedroom and one bathroom, along with its own kitchen, laundry facilities, and private entrance.

That arrangement offers visitors a place to stay with access to everyday essentials beyond a bedroom and bathroom. The listing also presents the space as an option for extended stays or additional living quarters.

Outside, the pool shares the property’s roster of amenities with a Jacuzzi, cold plunge, and sauna. A dedicated gym area adds another fitness feature.

The sales description identifies updates to the roof, heating and air-conditioning system, floors, lighting, and sliding doors. Landscaping and outdoor lighting have also been improved.

Other advertised features include reverse osmosis water filtration and smart entry technology. Parking consists of a gated motor court and an oversized garage with epoxy flooring.

The property is marketed near Runyon Canyon, with access to Hollywood and West Hollywood.

"Offering true tranquility amid the surrounding hills, this architectural retreat is just moments from Runyon Canyon, the best of West Hollywood, Hollywood, and beyond," the listing adds.

Gerber died Sept. 20 while staying at a rehabilitation facility in Santa Monica. Police investigated his death as a suspected overdose, and the medical examiner initially deferred the cause of death while further investigation was underway.

The reported suspicion should not be confused with a confirmed medical finding. Us Weekly’s account cited a police statement indicating that there was no evidence of foul play at that time.

Following his death, Crawford and Rande shared a touching tribute remembering their son’s kindness and vulnerability and thanking those who had offered support.

“Presley Walker Gerber. July 2, 1999-September 20, 2026. We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy," they shared in the joint statement.

His sister, model and actress Kaia Gerber, also shared an October tribute reflecting on her grief and their close relationship.

“Prez, I don’t have the words, and maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along. Words fail and words subtract and words summarize and words always lack truth. And how naive of me to believe that language could transcend grief. I’ve read all of the books and I have none of the answers. My articulation is no match against this, the magnitude of losing you. I am, quite literally, down on my f—ing knees," she penned.

Now publicly offered for sale, the Hollywood Hills property brings together a midcentury home, guest accommodation, and extensive outdoor amenities at an asking price just below $3.6 million.

#5574. Robert Pattinson Named the Next James Bond—Months After Joking His Beverly Hills Move Made Him ‘Bougie’

Robert Pattinson is taking over as James Bond—months after the British actor revealed that he and Suki Waterhouse had traded Los Angeles’ east side for a rental in Beverly Hills.

The 40-year-old will succeed Daniel Craig in the 26th Bond film, becoming the seventh actor to play 007 in the official series.

Denis Villeneuve will direct the still-untitled movie, with Steven Knight writing the screenplay and Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing. Craig last appeared as the British spy in 2021’s "No Time to Die."

Five months before the casting announcement, Pattinson told GQ that he, Waterhouse, and their young daughter were renting a house in Beverly Hills.

The move took him to a part of town where he said he’d never lived. In his earlier years in Los Angeles, he owned a large home in Los Feliz, which he eventually sold.

“I always thought I was an Eastside hipster guy. I would only ever come to Beverly Hills for my agency and stuff. Now I'm like, everything's kind of nice. Maybe I've turned bougie," he told the outlet.

One feature of the rental had a practical purpose: its home gym. Pattinson told GQ he was using it to train for "The Batman: Part II," the sequel to his 2022 debut as the superhero.

He recalled working out twice a day during preparations for his first turn as Batman and said that comments he’d made in interviews had given some people the wrong impression about how much he trained.

“[People said,] ‘You didn't work out at all.' I worked out every f—ing day. Even after that, I still look like I didn't work out. I worked out twice a day at, like, three o'clock in the morning," he told the outlet.

Pattinson has lived in Los Angeles on and off since his "'Twilight' years" in a "giant home that he wandered like a ghost," but his work still takes the family far from Beverly Hills.

He said his 2-year-old daughter had already joined Waterhouse on tour and accompanied him to film sets.

He also joked that fatherhood had changed his routine at home, where he now found himself going to bed far earlier than he used to.

The Batman sequel was set to shoot in London, and Pattinson said he had already looked into a possible school for his daughter while there.

The one that caught his attention was the school set up for the young actors on Warner Bros.’ new Harry Potter television series.

Pattinson has his own history with the franchise, having played Cedric Diggory before his breakout as Edward Cullen in "Twilight."

Bond will also reunite Pattinson with Villeneuve, who directed him in "Dune: Part Three." Before taking on 007, Pattinson had moved between major franchises and smaller films such as "Good Time" and "The Lighthouse."

His casting follows years of speculation about who would take over from Craig and marks the first Bond film since Amazon MGM Studios gained creative control of the franchise.

#5573. Lindsay Clancy’s Murder Retrial Set for March 2027—Inside the Massachusetts Home Where Her 3 Children Died

Lindsay Clancy is set to face a second murder trial on March 29, 2027—less than one year after her first case ended in a hung jury and more than three years after she was accused of murdering her three children inside the family's Massachusetts home.

Clancy, 36, has admitted to taking the lives of her daughter, Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan, but has pleaded not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges against her, with her attorneys arguing that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths.

Over the course of the five-week trial, her defense team sought to convince jurors that Clancy should not be held legally accountable for the killings because of a "lack of criminal responsibility," according to the Boston Globe.

Following 19 hours of deliberation, the 12-person jury was declared deadlocked after telling state Judge William Sullivan it was unable to reach a unanimous verdict. Sullivan instructed the jurors to return to the deliberation room and continue their efforts to reach a verdict, before eventually declaring a mistrial.

Then, mere weeks ago, Clancy returned to court, where her legal team attempted to argue that she can't be retried due to double jeopardy in hopes to have the charges dropped. Meanwhile, the prosecution asked the judge to decline the motion to dismiss the charges, claiming they could have a retrial.

Now, it has been revealed that the prosecution will be retrying Clancy on the same charges, with pretrial hearings scheduled for Dec. 30 and Feb. 18.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, previously claimed that he was ready to begin the retrial as soon as possible. He also requested President Donald Trump pardon Clancy; however, presidents can only pardon federal offenses.

Though Clancy was present in the courtroom in Plymouth, MA, she did not testify during the trial, which featured sworn testimony from dozens of witnesses, including her former husband, Patrick Clancy, medical professionals who treated her for mental health issues, and a former nanny who looked after her children.

The former nurse accused several medical providers of malpractice and negligence, claiming that she was repeatedly misdiagnosed, even as her symptoms continued to worsen. On the night of Jan. 24, 2023, she reportedly experienced suicidal hallucinations and heard a voice telling her that it was her "last chance" to kill herself and her children.

The prosecution, however, argued that she wasn't diagnosed with postpartum depression and that the murders seem premeditated, calling attention to the fact that Clancy had reportedly looked up ways to murder on her cellphone prior to the deaths of her children.

While her husband, Patrick, was picking up a takeout meal, Clancy strangled her children and tried to take her own life by cutting her neck and wrists, then throwing herself out of her bedroom window at the family's Duxbury, MA, home.

Cora and Dawson were pronounced dead that same night, while Callan died in the hospital a few days later. Lindsay survived her injuries, but was left paralyzed from the waist down.

Clancy's husband took to the stand to testify on behalf of his wife—as did the couple's former nanny, Elaine Rossi, who described the former nurse as a "wonderful mother."

"I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids," the nanny said, according to NBC10 Boston. "She cared for their safety, she was very concerned with Callan's eating and sleeping. She was a wonderful mother."

Rossi also told the court that Clancy had revealed to her she was "suffering from postpartum."

Patrick previously spoke out about his wife's horrifying crimes, sitting down with The New Yorker in October 2024 to defend her against critics, insisting that she was not "a monster."

At the time of the interview, the father of three explained that he had since relocated from Massachusetts to an apartment in New York City, quietly selling off the family's Duxbury home in an off-market deal.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with antidepressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Shortly after the deaths of his children, Patrick had issued a personal statement in which he asked the public to forgive his wife.

"A lot of people have said they can’t imagine and they’re right, there’s absolutely nothing that can prepare you," he wrote in the statement, which was shared on a GoFundMe page set up by his loved ones.

"The shock and pain is excruciating and relentless. I’m constantly reminded of them and with the little sleep I get, I dream about them on repeat. Any parent knows, it’s impossible to understand how much you will love your kids until you have them.

"The same goes for understanding the devastation of losing them. Cora, Dawson, and Callan were the essence of my life and I’m completely lost without them.

"My family was the best thing that ever happened to me. I took so much pride in being Lindsay’s husband and a dad to Cora, Dawson, and Callan. I always reminded myself that each day with them was a new gift."

He then shared touching tributes to each of his children, calling attention to his favorite things about them, including son Dawson's "bold, brown eyes" and daughter Cora's "infection laugh."

However, despite his grief, Patrick insisted that he had forgiven his wife, while urging the public to do the same.

"I want to ask all of you that you find it deep within yourselves to forgive Lindsay, as I have," he continued.

"The real Lindsay was generously loving and caring towards everyone—me, our kids, family, friends, and her patients. The very fibers of her soul are loving. All I wish for her now is that she can somehow find peace."

While the Clancy family home does not appear to have been listed for public sale since the tragic events unfolded inside it, Patrick revealed to The New Yorker that he had, in fact, sold it to an anonymous buyer, adding during the interview that he'd just been informed the sale has officially closed.

“There’s no house anymore,” he said. “There are no kids. All that’s left is me and Lindsay.”

He explained that he cleared out the house shortly after taking a solo trip to Central America and Europe in February 2024. He drove around his neighborhood gifting his children's stuffed animals and unused arcade cards to their friends.

Built in 1972, the home has been updated with refinished hardwood floors, a newer roof, and a redone kitchen with granite counters and new appliances and flooring. The three-bedroom, 1.5-bath interior spans 1,732 square feet with a remodeled extra room between the garage and kitchen.

The home sits on a tree-lined lot on almost an acre, with a deck, stone patio, and grassy lawn. The coastal town offers an "acclaimed" school system and a beautiful beach.

According to Realtor.com® records, the home last changed hands in 2018 for $500,000.

#5572. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5571. What Experts Forecast for Mortgage Rates and Home Prices in 2027

When it comes to housing, two of the biggest questions on everyone’s mind right now are:

And if you’re weighing whether to move in the next few months or wait until 2027, here’s what you should know.

When experts look ahead to 2027, they see a steady housing market. No wild swings. No big surprises. Just a calmer, more balanced market.

And steady makes planning a whole lot easier. Let’s break it down.

Lots of people are holding out for lower rates. But the latest forecasts from Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo show rates holding fairly flat through 2027 (see graph below):

Lenders see it the same way. In a recent survey from HousingWire, 70% of mortgage executives said they expect rates to be around 7.5% or higher six months from now (see graph below):

And if you’re wondering why, the answer is fairly simple. Chen Zhao, Head of Economics Research at Redfin, says:

“Until the underlying economic fundamentals—everything from oil prices to AI–that are keeping rates high change, mortgage rates are unlikely to fall significantly.”

So what does that mean for you? Instead of trying to guess where rates go next, focus on what you can control. Even if rates don’t budge, there are still ways to get the best rate possible. When you talk with your lender, ask about:

Your credit score. Even a small bump in your score could help lower your rate.

Different loan types. Some programs offer lower rates or smaller down payments than you might expect.

Buying down your rate. Paying a little more upfront (called “points”) can lower your rate and your monthly payment.

That way, you’ll know exactly where you stand and what a comfortable monthly payment looks like for you.

But what about prices? Here’s where steady really works in your favor.

Experts don’t see a home price drop coming. On average, forecasts from Fannie Mae, MBA, and Wells Fargo show prices rising about 1% to 1.5% a year through 2027 (see graph below):

In plain terms, in most places prices are still going up, just not as fast. For sellers, that means your home should hold onto its value. For buyers, slower growth gives you a little more breathing room. Just don’t count on prices getting cheaper while you wait.

But keep in mind, these are national forecasts. Prices can look very different from one area to the next, so what matters most is what’s happening where you live.

When the market is steady, you don’t have to try to time it perfectly. There’s no big swing to wait out.

That puts the focus back on you. Maybe you need more space for a growing family. Maybe you’re ready for less upkeep. A steady market makes it easier to plan for either one.

If you’re asking yourself should you move now or wait? You should know experts see a steady market through 2027, with rates holding near today’s levels and prices rising slowly. So, rather than waiting for a big shift that may not come, connect with a local real estate agent and run the numbers on what a move looks like at today’s rates and prices, so you can decide based on your goals instead of the headlines.

#5570. What Happened to Lindsay Clancy’s Home? How Duxbury House Was Quietly Sold to Former DA in Off-Market Deal Just a Year After Kids’ Deaths

Lindsay Clancy is set to face a second murder trial in March 2027—months after the jurors serving in the highly-publicized trial revealed they were deadlocked, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial, after an intense five-week courtroom showdown, during which they heard testimony from dozens of witnesses—and even visited the Massachusetts house where the former nurse is accused of murdering her children.

Clancy, 36, who did not testify in the case but was present in the Plymouth, MA, courtroom for the entirety of the trial, has admitted to taking the lives of daughter Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan.

However, she pled not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges she is facing, alleging that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths. On Sept. 4, the judge declared a mistrial.

Now, it has been revealed that she will be back in court in March 2027 to face a retrial on the same charges.

The trial began on July 31, when the jurors traveled to Clancy's former home in Duxbury, MA, where her three children were found in the basement by their father, Patrick Clancy, on Jan. 24, 2023, having been strangled with exercise bands.

According to the Associated Press, the jury was escorted into the home in groups of six and spent a total of 40 minutes at the property, walking through the entire abode, as well as the yard where Clancy was found after throwing herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt.

The visit took place just a few weeks after the property's new owner, former Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Michael C. Phippen, filed an objection to the juror viewing at a pretrial hearing in June, stating through his lawyer that it would be "massively disruptive" to his day-to-day life.

According to The Patriot Ledger, Phippen's attorney, Peter Maguire, told Judge William Sullivan, that his client's domestic partner would be home at the time of the visit, while also claiming that the jurors arriving at the property with their police escort would upset his pets, as well as his neighbors.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague, who is leading the prosecution team in Clancy's trial, noted that Phippen was made aware when he purchased the home that he may have to open it for a jury visit.

While Judge Sullivan overruled Phippen's objection, he put certain restrictions in place for the visit, limiting it to jurors, attorneys, and any court staff that were deemed necessary. He also barred any jurors from opening any closets or touching any of Phippen's personal items.

Phippen—who served as an assistant DA from April 2016 until December 2018, according to his LinkedIn page—purchased the home from Clancy's husband in an off-market deal in January 2024, almost a year to the day after the killings took place.

Property records show that he paid $675,000 for the three-bedroom dwelling, despite the fact that it was estimated to be worth closer to $800,000 at the time.

After Clancy's trial began, social media users began speculating that Phippen was involved in her case in some way, because it was being handled by the same District Attorney's office that he once worked for.

However, Phippen had not worked as an assistant DA for six years by the time he bought the property and his LinkedIn page shows that he established his own legal office in December 2018—and also now works as an attorney for Stark | Lattuca.

Other than the objection that he filed during the pretrial hearing, Phippen is not thought to have had any involvement in Clancy's trial. He has also never publicly discussed how he came to purchase the home.

The former nurse's husband, Patrick, first revealed that he had sold the property in October 2024, when he took part in an interview with The New Yorker, telling the outlet that he had offloaded the residence and relocated to an apartment in New York in the wake of his children's deaths.

He and Clancy had purchased the property for $500,000 in 2018, according to records.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with anti-depressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Closing arguments in Clancy's trial took place on Aug. 27, with the former nurse's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, reemphasized his argument that his client was in a "state of psychosis" when her children were killed, insisting that she cannot be found guilty of murder because of a "lack of criminal responsibility."

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect, as his honor instructed you, and they’re not going to be able to prove otherwise," he told the jury.

Prosecutor Sprague, however, said that—while there is no denying that Clancy was "suffering from mental illness and that she tried to kill herself"—the jury must decide what her state of mind was on the night that her children died.

"What's on trial here, what the issue is here is what Lindsey Clancy did the night of Jan. 24, 2023, and what her mental state was at the time," she said.

Sprague also claimed that witness testimony heard during the trial indicated that she was a "functioning mom" in the months leading up to the killings.

"You know that she knew the difference between right and wrong during that time," she added. "That’s a rational thought ... She knew it was wrong.

At the end of closing arguments, Judge Sullivan dismissed the jury to begin its deliberations, urging them to "have confidence" in the decision that they were being asked to make—whether Clancy was guilty of first-degree murder or the lesser charge of manslaughter.

"Please have confidence in what you're about to do, all right? I have that confidence in you," he said, according to NBC News. "I don't think I've ever seen a more dedicated group of jurors in any trial that I've ever been involved in."

It is not known exactly how long jury deliberations will take, however some legal experts have suggested that they could last for up to a week.

#5569. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. Talk to an agent about what's happening in your local market.

#5568. Provo Housing Market: Momentum Meets a Changing Market

As housing conditions shift, a market’s local economy offers an important starting point for understanding where the market is headed. In the Provo, Utah, metro, total nonfarm employment reached 324,000 payrolls in August, up 1.1% from a year earlier, while the unemployment rate declined to 3.4%.

That economic momentum is encouraging, but it is being tested by softer conditions in the housing market.

One important competitive dynamic is the relationship between new and existing home prices. As of July, the median new-home closing price was $495,800, compared with $541,000 for existing homes. That pricing relationship gives builders an avenue to compete with the resale market even as affordability remains challenging.

Sales conditions, however, are mixed. Annualized new-home sales totaled 4,594 units in August, down 6.1% year over year (YOY). Annualized detached sales increased 5.3% YOY, while attached sales declined 17.8%, underscoring different demand conditions by product type.

Supply is another increasingly important part of the story. Finished vacant inventory increased 18.9% YOY to 1,011 units as of Q2 2026. Zonda estimates the Provo market will be 3.89% oversupplied at year-end 2026.

The number of active detached new-home projects decreased roughly 1% YOY as of October while the number of active attached projects was flat. Total building permits are expected to decline by nearly 15% YOY in 2026.

Provo presents a market with two competing realities. Household and employment growth continue to support underlying housing demand, but elevated finished inventory, softer new-home sales, and affordability constraints argue for disciplined production. The projected decline in permitting could eventually help rebalance supply, but near-term execution will remain critical as builders compete for price sensitive buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.
