#5567. Court Report: Compass Attempts to Divide and Conquer in MLS War

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

A day after Compass sued 15 MLSs in separate lawsuits, the brokerage again made a move to divide and conquer in its campaign against several MLSs.

Facing a separate lawsuit brought by seven MLSs against Compass—including Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), bridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, REcolorado, MLSListings, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS—the brokerage submitted a letter on Nov. 13 to Southern District of New York Judge, Mary Kay Vyskocil, asking for a dismissal, or a motion to sever and transfer.

Within the filing, Compass alleges that the MLSs in question had sought an extension after the brokerage’s initial Oct. 6 letter, demanding that the organizations cease fining and punishing real estate professionals for “publicly marketing office exclusive listings or face an antitrust suit.”

The letter states that Mitch Skinner—an attorney acting on behalf of ARMLS, Doorify MLS and Hive MLS—spoke to Compass’s chief legal officer and asked for an extension to the demand letter’s deadline, on the grounds that “several decision makers were ill and others were busy and needed more time to work on Compass’ demand.” Later the filing mentions that the other MLSs separately sought extensions for time as well.

Compass allegedly extended the deadline, but accuses the MLSs of using that time to organize their Oct. 21 lawsuit against the brokerage instead of complying with Compass’s demands.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Compass’s attorneys argue that because the MLSs “(signaled) that a negotiated resolution was under consideration” by asking for extensions, the case should be dismissed.

Alternatively—should the motion to dismiss be denied—Compass requested that the court “sever each MLS’s claims and transfer them to the district where that particular MLS’s Home-District Action is pending.”

By separating each MLS plaintiff into distinct lawsuits, Compass seems to be holding true to its promise, where the brokerage would “spend millions of dollars to sue CRMLS and other MLSs to accomplish those goals,” as stated in the Sept. 8 letter sent to all the MLSs it sued.

Last week, the mega-brokerage Compass took a major step in the battle over listing restrictions by filing lawsuits against over a dozen MLSs, across eight states. Six of the MLSs are based in California, with three in North Carolina and the rest spread throughout a handful of other states around the country.

In one of Compass’s filed complaints—against North Carolina’s Hive MLS—the brokerage accuses the MLS of “using control of a home listing database that real estate agents in eastern North Carolina and the other areas Hive MLS services cannot work without,” to block Compass and protect the brokerage’s competitors.

Several of the MLSs targeted—including Hive MLS, ARMLS, REcolorado, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS and bridgeMLS—already sued Compass, asking a judge to preemptively declare their rules do not violate antitrust laws. They have characterized their various policies, which restrict how members can market listing off-MLS, as pro-competitive and pro-consumer, and claimed Compass is merely seeking to use its exclusive listings as a “competitive weapon.”

Compass, on the other hand, has repeatedly accused these MLSs of fighting purely to protect their own interests and claimed the MLS industry has long endured antitrust scrutiny from government regulators. It sent letters to many of these MLSs back in September, explicitly threatening to sue and force them to bear the legal costs if they continued enforcing the policies in question.

“It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” a Compass spokesperson said. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

While the lawsuits are filed against each MLS, the arguments broadly mirror Compass’s accusations against California-based CRMLS, which it separately sued back in October.

Compass moves to dismiss rent-monopoly allegations

Nearly four months since the case was originally filed, Compass now awaits a judge’s decision on its motion to dismiss the antitrust class-action lawsuit accusing the brokerage of monopolizing the rental market in New York City.

The case—initially filed by Peter Castaneda and Haley Gelfand—alleges that Compass monopolized the non-rent stabilized, multifamily residential real estate units (rental units) in its “conquest to seize control over various housing markets,” according to the original complaint, including efforts to remove Compass listings from New York’s StreetEasy portal.

“Compass, which now owns every other competitor real estate brokerage firm (referring to Anywhere Real Estate, which Compass acquired in January 2026), controls over 80% of the rental unit listings available for renters in Manhattan based on 2025 data,” the complaint continues. “Rather than compete in the relevant market on the merits to attain high profits, Compass instead neutralized Competitors by acquiring them.”

On Nov. 10, Compass submitted a motion to dismiss the plaintiffs’ complaint on the basis that they’ve failed to plead the “bedrock” requirement, failed to prove monopoly power and lacks antitrust standing.

Generally, the “bedrock” requirement refers to a plaintiff’s ability to prove a concrete injury was done, along with proving causation and redressability. Compass’s motion also argues that the renters are unable to prove that the brokerage holds monopoly power.

“By (the) plaintiff’s own account, it is the owners and managers of rental units who ‘set rent prices’ in response to supply and demand using various third-party ‘algorithms’ and ‘tools,’” Compass’ argument states. “The complaint does not allege that Compass owns, manages, or leases a single rental apartment, or that Compass sets rents or controls any of the pricing tools that landlords and owners use.”

But, the plaintiff’s original complaint alleges that Compass’ “campaign to have no competitors” is tied to the brokerage’s conduct when it comes to the publication of rental unit listings.

“Compass, led by its chief executive Robert Reffkin, has been engaged in both a litigative and public relations-based war with Zillow,” the complaint states. “The rerouting of Compass’ listings through REBNY Residential Listing Service (RLS) intentionally results in depriving consumers of free-to-access portals to find rental units and instead mandates the use of a broker to find a rental unit.”

The original complaint also argues that with control of over 80% of the listings in Manhattan alone, Compass can choose to delist them from free-to-use platforms like StreetEasy and thus drive up prices for other apartments listed due to the lack of supply.

While the case is still ongoing, all parties await the judge’s decision on the motion to dismiss.

After nearly 40 years of employment, the former chief financial officer of the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) filed a lawsuit against the association, accusing it of withholding his retirement benefit.

John Pierpoint—who retired from his role in 2025—filed the lawsuit against NAR in the Circuit Court of Cook County in Chicago last Wednesday.

According to a release from Pierpoint’s attorneys, NAR “improperly withheld one year of salary in retirement compensation despite having recorded the anticipated payment in its own financial records for more than a decade.”

The release also points out that NAR has maintained the executive retirement compensation practice for approximately two decades, and pays retiring senior executives a year’s worth of their base salary.

The amount Pierpoint was to receive for his retirement was about $541,000, or his base salary, according to his complaint. Pierpoint likens NAR’s refusal to pay his retirement benefit to their recent settlement in the Burnett lawsuit, where the association paid $418 million to plaintiffs.

Weighed down by the burden of the settlement and legal fees, Pierpoint’s attorneys argue that NAR “directed its finance staff to write the Compensation Reserve off its books, eliminating a liability of several million dollars from its balance sheet during the period in which it was funding its antitrust settlement obligations.”

“Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” David Fish, an attorney representing Pierpoint, stated. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives. We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees.”

#5565. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.

#5563. The Future of Home: 5 Trends for the Next 50 Years

What does the future of housing design look like? Much like with homes today, trends will be tied to how people live. To predict where design is headed, we need to consider how lifestyles are changing, identify which needs have staying power, and anticipate how homes might evolve to meet them.

DAHLIN Group assembled the top trends for the next 50 years to mark the firm’s 50th anniversary, reflecting on decades of design work to determine what the future looks like. According to DAHLIN, these will be key trends:

BUILDER spoke with DAHLIN’s Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, and Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, for their insight on why these trends will endure.

Fifty years is a long time to forecast residential design trends. How did you decide on these five trends, and what’s behind their staying power?

Wagner: A responsible 50-year view should not claim to know the exact layout, style, or construction method people will use. It should identify what future design must be able to do.

The common principle is agency: giving people more useful choices without requiring them to rebuild their lives or surroundings every time circumstances change.

The solutions to these needs will manifest in dramatically different ways over the next 50 years, but the needs themselves are unlikely to disappear.

How will wellness become more integrated?

Julian: Wellness will move deeper into the core decisions that shape everyday performance.

Daylight, window placement and performance, shading, material choices, air filtration, thermal zoning, and access to outdoor space will be considered together, rather than added as isolated features.

We also expect the idea of restorative space to become more distributed. A home does not need one wellness room if daylight, nature, movement, quiet, and thermal comfort are part of the daily path through the house. That makes wellness more relevant across housing types and price points.

The larger shift is from visible elements to a measurable and felt experience: cleaner air, better control, more useful daylight, a stronger relationship to the outdoors, and spaces that support both activity and retreat.

Design is already leaning away from fully open concept. How might this evolve?

Wagner: People want connection without constant exposure. The open plan still serves cooking, gathering, and shared family life extremely well, but a home now has to absorb more simultaneous activities. A call, homework, quiet conversation, and meal preparation may all happen at once.

People do not necessarily want more rooms; they want more control over how rooms relate.

These allow a space to borrow light and belong to the larger home when open, then become visually or acoustically distinct when needed.

Over time, this can make floor plans less defined. A room may shift between office, study, guest space, care space, or retreat because its boundaries and connections were designed to change.

The goal is not maximum openness at every moment. It is to give the homeowner control over when spaces participate in the life of the home and when they recede.

How will the design partnership with AI evolve?

Wagner: AI can already help teams generate and compare more early visual directions, translate abstract language into discussable imagery, and communicate a concept before investing in a complete visualization package. It can also help align a client and design team when they’re using the same word to mean different things.

The important limitation is that human expertise remains vital in framing the challenge, recognizing what is plausible, selecting the direction that serves the client best, and turning an evocative image into architecture that functions.

AI can quickly generate ideas and multiply options, but the designer must still decide which options deserve to move forward and turn them into a workable, real plan.

The near-term model is therefore collaborative. AI broadens the field of possibilities, while human experts frame the question, curate the outputs, and carry the selected idea into a coherent, buildable design.

Homeowners are placing greater importance on opportunities for social connection. How will future site and community planning support this?

Julian: Instead of relying only on a large destination facility such as a clubhouse or pool area, communities can offer a network of smaller lawns, gardens, play and sport areas, outdoor work settings, cafes or neighborhood retail, and places to sit along daily routes.

Smaller scale can also make participation easier and more approachable. It’s easier to join one of a few seats than to become the only person in a room designed for dozens. The same amount of common area can create more opportunities for connection when it’s placed closer to where people live and is shaped for different levels of participation.

When social space is woven into day-to-day patterns, community becomes a series of low-pressure encounters that can grow into familiarity and belonging.

Why will flexibility be the key to longevity in design?

Julian: Flexibility supports longevity when it reduces the cost and disruption of change. A room that has no assigned use may be flexible on paper, but true adaptability comes from practical decisions: useful daylight, appropriate openings, accessible routes, service relationships, and connections to indoor and outdoor space.

Those decisions determine whether a garage bay can credibly become an office or gym, or whether an ADU can serve a renter, a returning child, or an aging parent at different points in time.

The benefit is not that one design and layout lasts forever. It’s designing change into the bones of the home so that the home can adapt for a wide variety of family configurations without becoming obsolete.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5562. Inside Warren Buffett’s Surprisingly Modest Property Portfolio as He Steps Down as Berkshire Hathaway Chairman

Billionaire investor Warren Buffett has officially stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway—marking the end of an extraordinary era for the 96-year-old businessman, whose approach to real estate has long been almost as unconventional as his investing career.

Berkshire Hathaway announced on Sept. 18 that Buffett has been named chairman emeritus, effective immediately, while his son, Howard G. Buffett, has been elected chairman of the board. Buffett will remain a director and continue to offer his insight to the company.

“As Chairman Emeritus, Mr. Buffett will remain a member of the Board of Directors and will continue to offer his valued judgment and perspective,” Berkshire said.

The transition comes months after Buffett relinquished his CEO duties to longtime Berkshire executive Greg Abel, completing a carefully planned changing of the guard at the company Buffett has been associated with since 1965. Berkshire Hathaway sold $426 million more in stocks than it bought in the third quarter of 2026 under Abel. It was the 15th quarter out of the past 16 in which the company’s stock sales exceeded its purchases.

"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett said in a letter to shareholders, released alongside the announcement. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world."

Buffett isn't disappearing from Berkshire entirely. As chairman emeritus, he will remain on the company's board, while Howard takes over as chairman and Abel continues running Berkshire as CEO.

"Serving as your Chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted," Buffett wrote to shareholders while announcing the transition.

While Buffett's decades at Berkshire turned him into one of the wealthiest people on the planet, he has never amassed the sprawling collection of mansions and lavish vacation retreats often associated with billionaire status.

Instead, his property history is surprisingly limited—and anchored by the same Nebraska house he purchased nearly seven decades ago.

At the center of Buffett's real estate story is his longtime residence in Omaha, NE, which he purchased in 1958, when he was 28 years old.

Buffett paid just $31,500 for the five-bedroom property, which was built in 1921 and spans roughly 6,570 square feet. The home, where Buffett and his late wife, Susan Buffett, raised their three children, has remained his primary residence ever since.

Despite the enormous fortune he went on to accumulate, Buffett never traded the residence for a more extravagant billionaire compound.

The house has become closely associated with Buffett's famously restrained approach to spending, particularly when compared with the vast portfolios owned by many of his fellow billionaires.

The property is estimated to be worth about $1.44 million—a substantial increase from its 1958 purchase price, but still a relatively modest sum for a man whose fortune has climbed well into the billions.

Buffett has also made clear over the years that his attachment to the home goes beyond its financial value, repeatedly speaking about his satisfaction with the property rather than seeking out something larger or more luxurious.

Buffett's interest in properties began well before he purchased his Omaha residence.

As a teenager, the future billionaire used $1,200 of his savings to acquire a 40-acre Nebraska farm in 1944, making his first property investment at just 14 or 15 years old, depending on the timing of the purchase relative to his birthday.

Rather than working the land himself, Buffett arranged for a tenant farmer to operate it and split the proceeds—giving the budding investor an early lesson in owning an income-producing asset.

Decades later, he returned to farmland as an investment.

In 1986, Buffett paid $280,000 for a 400-acre Nebraska farm located north of Omaha, as per Architectural Digest.

The purchase further demonstrated his interest in land that could generate tangible, long-term returns rather than property acquired purely for status.

Buffett's land holdings extend beyond Nebraska and include farmland in Arizona and South Africa.

One of the biggest departures from Buffett's otherwise understated real estate history came in 1971, when he and Susan purchased a vacation home in the exclusive Emerald Bay community of Laguna Beach, CA.

They paid $150,000 for the property at a time when the surrounding area was far less developed than it is today.

Buffett later said the decision wasn't driven by an investment strategy—he bought the home because his wife liked it.

The three-level residence offered around 3,600 square feet of living space and six bedrooms, as well as a large deck with ocean views. Despite its coveted location, its interiors were relatively understated, with gray carpeting and white laminate kitchen countertops.

The property became a longtime family getaway, with Buffett and his family spending summers and Christmases there.

As the family expanded, so did their California footprint. Buffett acquired a neighboring residence to accommodate additional guests and connected the two properties with a staircase. He referred to the second house as the family's "annex."

But Buffett's connection to the California retreat began to fade after Susan died in 2004.

He sold the neighboring property in 2005 and ultimately decided to part ways with the original vacation house as well.

Buffett initially put his Laguna Beach residence on the market for $11 million in 2017—46 years after paying $150,000 for it.

By August 2018, the asking price had been reduced to $7.9 million. The property ultimately sold for that amount later that year, according to previous reporting on Buffett's real estate holdings.

Even at the reduced figure, the deal represented a dramatic increase over Buffett's original purchase price.

It also left his property portfolio without one of its few traditional luxury homes.

The Laguna Beach residence stood in stark contrast to the Omaha house that Buffett has steadfastly held on to throughout his ascent from ambitious young investor to one of the most influential figures in American business.

Now, as he relinquishes the Berkshire chairmanship he held for more than five decades, that Omaha residence remains one of the most enduring constants of his life.

#5560. Low Rates or Lots of Leverage? Buyers Rarely Get Both.

If you’ve been watching mortgage rates lately, you might feel a little stuck. Rates climbed above 7% this year, and a lot of buyers have decided to sit tight and wait for them to come back down.

But rates are only half the story. When you buy a home, you usually get one of two things: low rates or negotiating power. It’s rare to get both at the same time. And right now, you have a lot more of that second one than you might think.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. Rates were near 3%, and buyers rushed into the housing market. Those low rates sounded great, but they came with a catch. There were a lot of buyers just like you that you had to compete with – and there weren’t enough homes for sale to meet that demand.

That’s why homes got multiple offers, buyers paid over asking or waived inspections, and sellers held all the cards. Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com, shows just how one-sided things got:

“Seller’s markets peaked at 98 of 100 metros in spring 2022 after two years of mortgage rates near 3%.”

Then, in the second half of 2022, rates went up. As a result, the number of people buying homes went down, inventory grew, and the balance slowly started tipping from sellers back to buyers. Fast forward to today, and that flip is officially here.

In a recent report, Realtor.com found about two-thirds (66) of the top 100 metros now lean in favor of buyers (see graph below):

And while you may want lower rates, this shift in power has its own perks.

There are more homes for sale than there have been in years. And in a more buyer-friendly market like that, it means sellers have to work harder to get their homes sold. As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Higher inventory and lengthening days on market give buyers improved negotiating power.”

That shows up in the deals buyers are getting. According to Redfin, nearly half of buyers now get some kind of concession from the seller – like help with closing costs, money for repairs, or even the seller paying to buy down your mortgage rate (see graph below):

So when you find a home you love, even if the rate isn’t what you necessarily wanted, there are other levers to pull. Ask about a price cut or a seller-paid rate buydown, too. It could take some of the sting out of today’s rates.

And just in case you’re still thinking you’ll just hold off until rates drop, here’s what you should know. Experts at Fannie Mae, the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), and Wells Fargo don’t expect rates to fall much through 2027 (see graph below):

And here’s the whole point. Even if rates did drop in a big way, a lot of buyers would rush back in. More competition means fewer deals, fewer concessions, and sellers getting the upper hand again.

So waiting comes with a trade-off. You might land a better rate down the road, but you’d probably give up the bargaining power you have today.

That doesn’t mean you have to move right now. You should only buy when the numbers work for you. But if you’ve got a real reason to move, today’s leverage could help make your numbers work – even at today’s rates.

#5559. More Roofing Choices Without More Complexity

For roofing professionals, the expectations surrounding a roofing project continue to expand. A roof is no longer evaluated solely on its ability to protect homes from the elements. In addition to standing up to increasingly unpredictable weather, roofing products are expected to deliver lasting value while complementing and even elevating the architectural style and character of a home.

With greater regularity, roofing professionals are learning to navigate a market where performance expectations, design preferences, and project requirements have become more challenging.

It’s a combination of factors that has made flexibility increasingly important. A roofing solution that works well for one architectural style or climate may not be the right fit for another. There’s a growing need to access materials that can meet a range of aesthetic preferences and performance demands, while homeowners want the confidence that their choices will provide both the protection they expect and the look they envision.

Against that backdrop, a roofing brand called US Tile is bringing two established roofing materials—concrete and clay—together under a single, made-in-the-U.S. portfolio. The aim is to offer a more comprehensive selection of tile roofing options while simplifying the process of navigating those choices.

Benefits of Concrete and Clay From a Single Source

Rather than looking across multiple sources to find the right combination of styles, profiles, colors, and performance characteristics, roofing contractors and builders can explore a broader portfolio within a unified offering.

Some projects may call for the versatility and design range of concrete, while others may benefit from the distinctive character of clay. With both materials represented within the same portfolio, there’s greater flexibility to match a roof to the look of the home, the preferences of the homeowner, and the durability demands of the local environment.

Beyond aesthetics, having access to concrete and clay roofing from the same manufacturer makes it easier to spec and offer homeowners two energy-efficient, Class A fire-rated materials that hold up to prolonged exposure to the elements and extreme weather.

More Productive Conversations Between Roofing Professionals and Homeowners

A broader range of materials and possibilities can make homeowner discussions more fruitful. Instead of starting with a limited set of materials and working backward from what is available, offering concrete and clay from the same source means each project can be approached with a wider range of potential solutions. There’s more opportunity to balance appearance, performance, budget, and other project considerations without unnecessarily complicating the specification process.

A unified portfolio can result in simplified access to product information and support while reducing some of the hurdles that can arise when coordinating different materials and suppliers. Across multiple busy projects, those efficiencies can matter just as much as the products themselves.

A Broader Portfolio and Greater Design Flexibility

Ultimately, combining concrete and clay roofing under one made-in-the-U.S. brand is about giving professionals more ways to meet the demands of their projects. A broader portfolio allows for greater design flexibility, while the performance characteristics of concrete and clay tile roofing help address homeowners’ growing expectations for resilience and long-term value.

With more options and a more streamlined path to finding them, roofing professionals can approach each project with greater confidence—and homeowners can have more faith in their next roof as a smart long-term choice that adds value and peace of mind.

#5558. More Than a Closing: The Growing Role of Financial Services in Home Building

Historically, financial services have occupied a relatively straightforward role in the home builder business model. Mortgage, title insurance, and related services could generate ancillary revenue while helping buyers move from contract to closing.

Today, that traditional role has shifted amid a challenging affordability environment, mounting pressure on margins, and heightened buyer expectations. Financial services have elevated from an adjacent business opportunity to a more strategic part of the home building platform.

The question is increasingly not simply how much revenue these services can generate, but how they can help builders sell homes, create a more consistent home buyer experience, and operate more efficiently at scale.

Mortgage services may provide the most obvious example. With mortgage rates recently returning to the 7% range, affordability remains a defining challenge for the industry. In September, 66% of builders surveyed by the National Association of Home Builders reported using sales incentives. Zonda similarly reported that more than 80% of new-home communities offered incentives on quick move-in homes in August.

In that environment, financing is no longer simply what happens after a buyer decides to purchase a home; rather, it becomes a core part of what makes the purchase possible in the first place.

It may be with this in mind that large builders have placed such emphasis on their mortgage capabilities. For example, two of the nation’s largest public builders recently reported mortgage capture rates above 80%, underscoring how closely financing has become integrated with the home sale.

The strategic value goes beyond capturing mortgage revenue. An effective financing platform gives builders another lever to address affordability, tailor incentives, and help qualified buyers get across the finish line.

The same strategic thinking increasingly applies to title, settlement, and other services surrounding the transaction.

Consider title and closing. These services sit at a critical point in the home buyer journey: the moment when months of searching, financing, construction, and anticipation culminate in ownership.

For the buyer, those distinctions between companies and functions may matter very little. The mortgage process, communications leading up to closing, signing experience, and delivery of the keys can all become part of a single perception of the builder’s brand. Delivering a consistently superior closing experience becomes an increasingly important element of how buyers remember the home builder.

For builders operating across multiple markets, however, delivering consistency can be difficult. Growth through geographic expansion or acquisition can leave behind fragmented networks of local providers, processes, and systems.

“What works well across a handful of communities can become much harder to manage across dozens of markets and thousands of closings,” says Anne Law, president of First American Title’s Homebuilder Services Division. “That’s why builders are increasingly looking at financial services as a scalable platform with consistent processes, strong underwriting, and an excellent closing experience, rather than a collection of individual transactions.”

Importantly, a more integrated strategy does not necessarily mean bringing every capability in-house. Builders are placing greater emphasis on capital efficiency and asset-light operating models, and those same principles now drive decisions on how they approach financial services.

The objective is not necessarily ownership. It is control over the things that matter most: the customer experience, service standards, data visibility, operating consistency, and economics. Scale adds another consideration. Licensing, regulatory requirements, and operating standards can vary across jurisdictions, adding complexity as builders expand into new markets. Experienced financial services partners like First American Title can provide infrastructure and expertise to help navigate those requirements.

That creates room for a range of models, including wholly owned operations and strategic partnerships. The right structure will vary by builder, service, and market. What matters is whether the model balances control, investment, and operating responsibility while supporting scalable growth, regulatory compliance, and a consistent customer experience.

From Ancillary Revenue to Strategic Infrastructure

The evolution of financial services ultimately reflects a broader change in how builders compete.

When affordability is strained, financing can help sell the home. When buyers expect a seamless process, well-executed and consistent title and closing services can reinforce and enhance the home-buying experience. And when builders operate across expanding footprints, standardized financial-services relationships can create greater consistency, visibility, and efficiency.

Revenue matters. But there are other parts of the equation that are important. For example, builders today are closely examining how mortgage, title, and settlement fit into the broader operating model and whether those capabilities are structured to support the next stage of growth.

In that sense, financial services are becoming less ancillary to the home building business and more integral to how modern builders sell, serve, and scale.

#5557. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

If you're active duty, you've served, or you know someone who has, connect with a local agent and a trusted VA-approved lender to see what you qualify for.Your VA home loan benefit and today's market could be a powerful combination.

#5556. Inside Dolly Parton’s Eclectic Property Portfolio and Legacy as the Music Legend Receives Posthumous Grammy Nods

Dolly Parton has left behind a legacy that will continue to grow for years to come.

The music legend—who passed away following a brief battle with cancer at the age of 80 on Aug. 25—was recently honored by the Recording Academy, receiving three posthumous nominations ahead of the 69th Annual Grammy Awards.

The "9 to 5" hitmaker has received two nominations in the Best Country/Duo Group Performance category for "Light of a Clear Blue Morning" with Lainey Wilson, Reba McEntire, Miley Cyrus, and Queen Latifah, and her "Butterfly" collaboration with the Zac Brown Band.

Parton's memoir, "Star of the Show: My Life on Stage," has also received a nod in the Best Audio Book, Narration, and Storytelling Recording category.

As Parton's contributions to the entertainment industry continue to receive their deserved recognition, it's worth noting another talent the country icon showcased throughout her lifetime: property investment.

To honor the country icon, Sept. 25 was hailed as "Dolly Parton day," and is set to be celebrated all across the country with parades, library fairs, community singing, and more.

Many hailed her on-stage talents, her generosity of spirit, and her philanthropic work—something that she demonstrated even through her love of property investment when she donated a longtime home to charity in 2023.

Parton's homes also provided her with a much-needed sanctuary, a place where she was able to retreat from the glare of the public spotlight and savor a private life at home with her husband, Carl Dean, who passed away in March 2025.

Indeed, despite her enormous celebrity profile, the "Jolene" singer still managed to keep her personal life at home largely hidden from the public, particularly when it came to the Brentwood, TN, estate she and Dean shared for years.

Parton also attempted to shield the public from her private health struggles—admitting earlier this year that she had neglected her own wellbeing while caring for Dean at the end of his life, but insisting that she was receiving the help she needed.

It was only revealed after news of her passing was announced that she had been quietly battling cancer, although it is not known what type she had been diagnosed with.

Parton's death was shared in an Instagram post on her personal account, which featured a video filmed by her nephew Bryan Seaver.

"My name is Bryan Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis, and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he said.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it til now."

He added: "Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."

Seaver went on to praise his aunt as someone who "lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents, and countless others." He did not share a cause of death.

"A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family," an obituary shared with Realtor.com® reads.

"Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place.

"Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact."

Hours after the news of her death was revealed, the late singer's family shared that she had spent her final days being treated for cancer.

“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand," the statement read.

It continued, "“Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones."

Parton's death marks the end of an extraordinary life and career, one that also saw her build an impressive real estate empire that reflected her Tennessee roots and her superstar status.

Before she became a country music legend with a sprawling real estate portfolio, Parton was one of 12 children growing up in a tiny, rustic cabin tucked away in the Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee.

Parton spent her childhood in a one-bedroom cabin in Locust Ridge, which is situated just outside of Sevierville, TN, and had no electricity or running water, according to records.

Parton was born on Jan. 19, 1946 to Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. in Pittman Center, TN. The songstress and her siblings, Willadeene, David, Coy, Robert Jr., Stella, Cassie, Randy, Larry, Floyd, and twins Freida and Rachel, all grew up in the humble home.

Although the property where she was raised is not available for fans to visit, they can gawk at a replica, which the country star recreated at her Dollywood theme park, which is located in Pigeon Forge, TN, and boasts “original treasures” from her early days.

The replica was constructed by Parton's brother, Bobby, and received a thumbs up from the country star's mom.

Outside, there is a sign that reads, “These mountains and my childhood home have a special place in my heart. They inspire my music and my life. I hope being here does the same for you! Dolly.”

Although fans are not able to tour the grounds of the home where she was raised, they can still enjoy the city sights and view the statue of the country legend at the Sevier County Courthouse’s lawn.

In 2007, Parton and her husband purchased the two-bedroom, two-bathroom property for $1.2 million, but it never served as her main residence.

She then listed the home for sale for $1.4 million in 2014—although records show that it only changed hands in 2023, when it sold for $1.2 million. It's unclear whether Parton quietly offloaded the home before its most recent sale.

Then, in July 2026, the property hit the rental market for $12,000 a month.

Built in 1923, the property sprawls across 1,091 square feet and offers guests a "rare opportunity to lease the legendary former home of Dolly Parton," per the listing, which is held by Richard Schulman of KW Westside Estates.

Situated in the heart of the city's Design District, the fully furnished home perfectly marries vintage charm with modern finishes while placing residents just steps away from Melrose Avenue, Santa Monica Boulevard, trendy restaurants, boutique shopping, and nightlife.

Upon entering the property, guests are greeted with an open floor plan that shows off the expansive living area and kitchen.

The living room boasts plenty of lounging space as well as a cozy fireplace for guests to enjoy on California's chilly evenings.

Moving into the chef's kitchen, there is wraparound marble counter that matches the patterned backsplash. The cuisine center also boasts state-of-the-art appliances.

"Inside, the open-concept living area is filled with natural light and stylish finishes, flowing into an updated kitchen with stainless steel appliances and designer tile," the listing notes.

The primary bedroom features enough room for a king bed and a seating area. It also boasts a glamorous walk-in closet, an en suite bath, and easy access to the lush backyard.

The second bedroom is just as charming thanks to its own private covered balcony. The property also boasts a humble laundry room, complete with seating areas.

Moving outside, there's a perfect entertaining area thanks to an open-air kitchen, a dining area, patio, and covered deck.

"Outdoor spaces include a tropical-inspired patio and covered deck ideal for dining and entertaining," reads the listing, which states that the property is available from Aug. 15, 2026.

The property's description also calls attention to the home's ideal proximity to many of Los Angeles' most interesting communities, stating: "This coveted neighborhood is known for its walkability, creative energy, and long-standing ties to entertainment and cultural history."

Parton and Dean owned a mountainside sanctuary for decades before she decided to gift it over to the Ronald McDonald House Charities of Southern California, which offloaded it in July 2024, according to records.

The same month Dean passed away, the home was put back on the market for $770,000—just one year after it was sold for $585,00 by a charity that the musician donated it to in November 2023.

Just 30 days after being listed, the property was sold for above asking for $800,000.

Before being snapped up, the listing called attention to the singer, describing the home as "Dolly Parton's former Idyllwild retreat—a home as iconic as the legend herself."

"If walls could sing, this charming three-story mountain retreat would be belting out a country classic," the description continues, noting that "nearly everything inside remains just as Dolly left it."

Indeed, the property is filled with many of the personal items and collectibles that sat in the dwelling when Dolly last occupied the home, having used it as an escape for many years—although several modern updates have been made in the eight months since it last changed hands.

The listing noted that the home has been outfitted with a new luxury shingle roof, while an electric vehicle charger was also installed in order to add another layer of convenience, particularly given the home's rather remote location.

Still, the new owners took pains to ensure that Parton's presence remains in every room, with the listing photos revealing that a tea set has been placed on the kitchen table, along with printed instructions addressed "to Dolly, from Steve," which detail how to make the perfect brew.

Elsewhere in the home, various knickknacks, including framed art, collectible plates, and various pieces of china can be seen adorning wooden shelves that run throughout many of the wood-paneled rooms.

A signed photo of Parton in her youth hangs on one of the walls, while one of the bathrooms has been outfitted with a guitar-shaped toilet seat for an added homage to her musical career.

Multiple fireplaces can be found in the living spaces and in the primary bedroom, adding a cozy feel to the 1,800-square-foot property.

Intriguingly, though the home now—quite literally—screams "Dolly Parton," her ownership of the property remained a closely guarded secret for many years and was only brought to light when it was sold in July 2024.

According to property records, the cabin was originally built in 1996, before being sold for just $126,000 in December 1994, which is when Parton is believed to have purchased it.

The "Jolene" hitmaker and Dean snapped up another quaint California house in 2004 and owned it for a decade, before quietly offloading it in 2014, when it sold for $940,000.

Located "in the heart of" the Danish-inspired town of Solvang, the adorable mini compound, which still retains many of the features added by the country music star during her ownership, features three petite properties: a main residence and two rental units.

"This one-of-a-kind property features the country legend's original, authentic 'Wig Room,'" state the listing for the home, which was being sold by its current owner, Chris Lapp.

A plaque stationed at the front of the dwelling proudly signals its impressive heritage as the "former home of Dolly Parton: singer, actress, and American icon," while a stained-glass window above the front door of the property's main residence features the legend's name, along with a butterfly.

However, one of the more eye-catching details at the front of the property has nothing to do with Parton at all, but rather pays tribute to Solvang's longstanding ties to Denmark and Europe: a miniature windmill that has been painted to match the home's distinctive gray, white, and red color palette.

Lapp, who bought the property in 2022 for $1.3 million, explained to SFGate that he'd heard Parton was inspired to purchase the dwelling because it "reminded her of her grandmother's home."

Meanwhile, local resident and business owner Wes Leslie noted that the songstress may well have "hung on to" the dwelling as an "investment property," although he said it has also been rumored that she had family who used the home.

After he bought the home, Lapp spent a great amount of time restoring it to its original glory—and said that he has ensured the tenants who currently live in the rental units have not made any significant changes to its interiors, many of which he believes were curated by Parton herself, including several heart stencils on the walls.

Beyond the special touches that Parton incorporated throughout the home, the property features a number of very unique features across all of its spaces: a three-bedroom, two-bathroom main house, a three-bedroom, two-bathroom rear unit, and a one-bedroom lower unit, all of which offer "private patios and off-street parking."

Upon entry to the main residence, which has a cheerful red front door, visitors will find a bright, airy living room, a small, yet well-equipped kitchen, and three comfortable bedrooms.

The aforementioned "wig room" has been outfitted with an enormous mirror and a built-in vanity perfect for trying on different styles—however, a future occupant could easily use this space as a flex room or office.

Featuring large windows throughout, the property gets ample natural light—while the sun-soaked patio space provides another charming area for guests to relax and kick back.

For those eager to turn their next property investment into a lucrative business opportunity, the home's impressive history as a successful rental will no doubt be one of its most appealing features. According to the listing, it generated a "gross annual income of $116,000" via the rental units—which are both tenant-occupied.

Dean and Parton met on the day that she moved to Nashville when she was just 18 years old—bumping into one another outside of the Wishy Washy Laundromat, according to the Associated Press.

Two years later, the couple tied the knot in a heartfelt ceremony in Ringgold, GA, and opted to stay out of the spotlight, tucking away at their ultraprivate Nashville home where they lived throughout the entirety of their marriage.

The couple spent their days in a five-bathroom property that sits on 63 acres and is informally known as Willow Lake Plantation.

Although it's unknown how much the couple splashed out for the property, Realtor.com estimates that the property is now worth $8.8 million.

In 2014, Parton garnered approval from the Brentwood board to build a barn on the property that "architecturally matches" the other three barns on the residence and doesn't exceed 17 feet in height.

Because of the couple's bid for a private life, little is known about their two-story property.

Although Dean decided to remain out of the public eye, he frequently inspired his wife's career, most notably influencing her hit song "Jolene."

In 2008, Parton told NPR that the song came to life after a bank teller developed a "terrible crush" on Dean.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband, and he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention.

"It was kind of like a running joke between us when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one," she explained.

Their marriage has long been a hot topic as Dolly previously revealed that they have an emotionally "open marriage," and that she had even developed feelings for another man.

In 2017, Parton revealed in her book "Dolly on Dolly: Interviews and Encounters with Dolly Parton" that she developed crushes on other men while married.

"I've had crushes on some very unusual men, but Carl knows I'll always come home, and I'm not having sex with these people, I'm just flirting and having fun.

"Yes, it's an open relationship, but not sexually, and I would kill him if I thought he was doing that.' He would shoot me too. At the end of the day, we love each other madly.

"I think so much of it is the fact that we are honest and open, and we have a warped sense of humor!" the singer explained while speaking to BBC.

Parton has also previously revealed that the couple opted to not have kids because she didn't believe "God" meant it for her.

"Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom, so I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work."

"I didn't have children because I believed that God didn't mean for me to have kids so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like Imagination Library because if I hadn't had the freedom to work, I wouldn't have done all the things I've done. I wouldn't be in a position to do all of the things I'm doing now," Parton said in a 2020 episode of "The Oprah Conversation"

She added that she has made "sacrifices" but is doing what she is "supposed to do."

"I've made sacrifices, but I think, like I said, I believe what I know I'm supposed to do,” she said of her purpose.

#5555. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? Talk to a local real estate agent.

#5554. EXCLUSIVE: Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg Sell Longtime Illinois Home for $2.6 Million

Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg have sold their Illinois residence for $2.6 million—two months after listing the sprawling St. Charles property for $2.8 million.

The singer, 57, and the actress, 53, owned the residence for more than a decade, having purchased it for $1.1 million in 2015.

Built in 1996, the four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home spans 7,236 square feet and sits on 1.26 acres.

Described as "an extraordinary St. Charles estate," the property underwent extensive renovations during Wahlberg and McCarthy's time there, with the couple transforming it into a personalized retreat designed for both entertaining and relaxing.

Inside, the home boasts an expansive living room and family room, a formal dining room, den, game room, recreation space, exercise room, and finished lower level.

The kitchen comes with an island, breakfast bar, walk-in pantry, and butler's pantry, while hardwood and stone flooring can be found throughout much of the main level.

Adding to the home's cozy appeal are six fireplaces, which are spread throughout spaces, including the living room, family room, primary bedroom, and basement.

The primary suite serves as its own private retreat and features an en suite bathroom with a soaking tub, double sinks, and a full-body spray shower.

However, some of the property's most impressive amenities can be found in its entertainment and wellness spaces.

The lower level features a bar and recreation areas, while the home also comes equipped with an exercise room and sauna.

"The reimagined English basement offers an entire recreation level with a home theater, sauna, cold plunge, bar, and generous gathering spaces," the listing read.

Outside, the couple created a resort-style setup with a swimming pool, waterslide, waterfall, spa, putting green, expansive patios, and lush landscaping.

#5553. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. #5551. Navigating the AI Shift

https://www.lamacchiarealty.com/leadership/kim-beaulieu

Regions served: Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Vermont, Maine and Florida

Years in real estate: 14 Number of offices: 29 Number of agents: 840, plus 81 employees

What AI developments do employees and agents need to be paying attention to?

The big one is knowing which models give you facts and which ones are people pleasers. Take listing remarks, for example. ChatGPT is excellent at them, but you need strict guardrails on it, because a people-pleaser model prioritizes making you happy over the facts and the rules. Left alone, it will write you a Fair Housing violation and never tell you it did. Beyond that, ask the questions most people skip: How are my competitors using it? How are my vendors using it?

Give us your top tips for HR leaders as they prepare people to successfully navigate the AI shift.

First, keep an open mind, because AI is the newest employee at your business. In addition to needing policies and procedures to follow, it also needs training and oversight just like an employee does. Second, give current employees the chance to utilize AI, and when making future employment decisions, build AI capability into job descriptions. Third, have employees use the paid versions, making sure they’re turning off the learning capabilities. Otherwise, competitors could unintentionally learn closely guarded secrets.

At Lamacchia, we’ve been working on some larger projects and shipping quicker wins along the way. We recently released a branding tool agents install into their own AI, so anything they generate comes out compliant with our brand standards automatically. The next one in beta testing translates forms, documents and flyers into any language.

How will AI change the way brokerages approach recruiting, onboarding, training and employee development?

Real estate is a people business, and the relationship part is the part AI doesn’t touch, but everything around it changes. Recruiting is already moving that way. Sourcing, screening, scheduling, the first follow-up are all getting automated. My caution as an HR professional is that you still own the outcome. If a vendor’s tool screens someone out, that’s your decision, and you need to be able to explain how it was made. Onboarding is where you can save administrative time. New people ask the same 20 questions in their first week, and they ask them at night and on weekends when there’s nobody there to answer. AI answers instantly, and it answers the same way every time. Training and development are where the real gains are. With AI, you can give every agent individualized coaching. You can let them practice a listing presentation, review their own scripts, get feedback at 10 p.m. when they actually have time. None of that replaces person-to-person interactions, but it helps bridge gaps.

What role do you see HR playing in helping people adapt, learn and take advantage of new technologies?

HR has to be at the table early. Historically, HR gets brought in at the end of a technology decision to write the policy after somebody else already picked the tool. With AI, that’s backwards, because almost every risk is a people risk. HR needs to be part of the decision, not the cleanup.

The second piece is making it safe to learn. People won’t experiment with something they think is going to replace them. If your employees believe AI is a threat, they’ll quietly avoid it, and you won’t find out until you’re two years behind. HR helps set that tone.

Third is guardrails: policies, approved tools, what can and can’t go into a prompt, what gets reviewed before it leaves the building. This gives people something to work inside of so they’re not figuring it out alone and making different decisions than you would about your data.

For more information, please visit https://www.lamacchiarealty.com.

Paige Tepping is RISMedia’s senior managing editor.

#5549. Noah Kahan Says ‘Life Goes On’ After Grammys Snub—Inside the Vermont Town the Artist Calls Home When He Wants to Escape Nashville

Noah Kahan had a very levelheaded response to his apparent snub from the 69th Annual Grammy Awards.

The singer-songwriter received only one nomination from the organization, securing a nod for best contemporary folk album for “The Great Divide: The Last of the Bugs”—the deluxe edition of his fourth studio album, which explores his complicated feelings toward leaving and eventually returning to his hometown of Strafford, VT.

Kahan’s exclusion from the most prominent categories of the awards show—album of the year, record of the year, and song of the year—has come as a surprise to the music industry.

“Life goes on,” Kahan, 29, said in a Nov. 16 social media post shared shortly after the nominees were announced.

While the statement is vague, it’s an apparent response to a comment he made the night before the highly anticipated nominations were rolled out.

“Whatever happens tomorrow I love you all and I have done everything I’ve ever needed to in my career because of YOUR support,” he wrote in a Nov. 15 X post.

Kahan’s response isn’t entirely surprising, as he’s often shared his candid feelings about the music industry and his newfound fame.

In the 2026 Netflix documentary “Noah Kahan: Out of Body,” the star speaks at length about the ways in which his life has changed as his career has grown. Perhaps one of the most tangible differences was a move to Nashville, TN.

Kahan and his now-wife, Brenna Nolan, whom he has been with for more than a decade, purchased a home in Music City for its proximity to the industry.

While the couple tend to keep their home life private, they did share quite a bit of the home in the documentary, particularly the backyard where their beloved dog, Penny, digs lots of holes, the generously sized porch Kahan enjoys playing guitar on, and the room dedicated to an at-home golf simulator that he joked shows just how “out of touch” he’s become.

At the time the documentary was filmed in 2024, Kahan and Nolan had recently moved to Tennessee.

“We moved from a one-bedroom apartment in Boston to here, and it was really jarring,” Nolan explained.

“It’s a huge change, and it’s a lot to deal with,” Kahan agreed. “We’ve tried to make it feel as much like Vermont as we can.”

The cameras certainly captured a few of the home’s New England-inspired decor, including a funky fawn print runner that decorates the stairs and a gallery wall with a Vermont license plate prominently displayed.

While the home’s beautiful interiors didn’t get quite as much screen time as most interior design-obsessed viewers may have wanted, there is one tiny Easter egg that gives a bit more color: a special thanks to Corey Morris Studios, a Nashville-based firm that specializes in “timeless, functional spaces rooted in traditional style and executed with a modern flair,” per their Instagram account.

Owner Corey Morris thanked Kahan for the shoutout in an April 2026 Instagram post.

“Never expected in a million years to see my name in a Netflix special!” he wrote. “One of the greatest honors of my career has been helping make the family’s Nashville house feel like home.”

Although Kahan did his best to bring the Vermont vibes down South, it seems as if no amount of home decor could replicate what he loves most about Strafford.

During a trip up North, Kahan explained that when he’s in Vermont—which is where he feels most at home—there’s less pressure around his career.

“Being here ... no one’s like, ‘What’s next, Noah?’ You know? It’s never about me as much as it is down in Nashville, which I like,” he said in the documentary. “I do love Nashville. I love the people I have down there. But like, it’s all my career, all the time. Everyone around me is a musician. Everyone around me is working on music. When I’m here, I feel like I’m in my home.”

The special also followed Kahan to New York City, where he previously lived at one point.

“I loved the memories I had here, but I just felt like I wasn’t meant to be in New York,” he explained. “I had expectations of myself. I thought living in a city would make me be social and, like, want to go outside and, like, go do things. It was a place where I was at my most burnt-out.”

In fact, Kahan spends much of the hour and 34 minutes of “Out of Body” grappling with his apparent discomfort just about everywhere he’s lived, given the stark contrast between each of the locations.

“I wonder if I can actually be fully satisfied in any setting at all,” he questioned. He added that he felt “suffocated” by his pre-fame life in Vermont and New Hampshire, but “yearned” for the “simplicity” when he left.

“You can't just escape who you are because you moved to a different place,” he said. “That’s not how it f-cking works.”

Towards the end of the documentary, Kahan and Nolan are seen driving through Strafford, taking a look at homes with “for sale” signs out front.

“We’re trying to make an imminent move back to where we’re from,” he said. “Looking for our next place, and coming back home, basically.”

On that note, it’s not a surprise that the newlyweds have yet to confirm if they’ve purchased a new abode in Strafford.
