#5532. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5531. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5530. Newrez Launches Personal Loans, Powered by Upgrade

Newrez—the residential mortgage lender and servicer—announced the launch of Newrez Personal Loans, powered by Upgrade. The new offering expands the financial tools available to eligible Newrez homeowners, providing access to funds for a variety of financial needs, such as debt consolidation, home improvements and unexpected expenses.

According to a release, personal loans are available through a partnership with Upgrade—a financial technology company that offers consumer credit products—and are issued by Upgrade’s bank partner, Cross River Bank.

“Our relationship with homeowners doesn’t begin and end with a mortgage,” Newrez CCO Leslie Gillin stated. “Homeowners’ financial needs often extend beyond their monthly mortgage payment, and we’re proud to broaden the ways we can support them, including helping identify opportunities for savings as they navigate important financial decisions. Partnering with Upgrade is another example of us delivering on our mission to do everything possible to make home happen.”

“Consumers increasingly expect financial solutions to be fast, transparent and easy to access,” said Avia Kay, Upgrade’s senior vice president of marketing. “We’re excited to partner with Newrez to help homeowners explore personal loan options through a simple online experience, supported by the trust Newrez has earned with its customers. Together, we’re making it easier for eligible homeowners to access funding quickly when they need it.”

For more information about Newrez Personal Loans, powered by Upgrade, visit here.

#5529. Jennifer Lopez Celebrates ‘Freedom’ as an Empty Nester Since Her Twins Left California Home for College

Jennifer Lopez has admitted that she is enjoying the "freedom" that comes with living alone after her 18-year-old twins, Max and Emme, left their California home for college.

The 57-year-old singer and actress—who is attempting to sell her and ex-husband Ben Affleck's $50 million marital mansion—once again opened up about the realities of being an empty nester while appearing on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon."

The singer, who shares the twins with ex-husband Marc Anthony, admitted that she "cried for six months straight" when her twins headed off to college.

Although Lopez confessed it has been "emotional," she insisted it has also been an "amazing" journey.

“It’s all the feelings. It’s like one of those moments in life where you’re just, you’re sad, you’re melancholy, but you’re excited and you’re hopeful—there’s just so many feelings that go with [it]. I cried for, like, six months straight, like, two months before they graduated until I dropped them off and then a few weeks after that," she said.

“It’s crazy ... like, I still have on my phone them on my lap, as babies," she added. "It goes so fast, just like everybody says.”

The A-lister admitted that she is now getting comfortable with the "freedom" she has living alone.

“It’s the first [time] since I was, I don’t know, in my early 20s that I haven’t been with someone, had my kids. I’m alone, I’m free—I can do whatever the f--- I want! And it’s kind of amazing, but also weird," she joked.

In October, Lopez said she was channeling that “devastation” into her music.

Speaking to Variety, the hitmaker revealed that living alone has inspired a burst of songwriting, producing material she believes could become some of her biggest hits.

“They take up such a big part of your brain for so long, and when they’re gone, which is devastating and sad and scary, you’re facing a life that’s totally different now, and you’re like, ‘What am I going to do with this space and this time?’" the hitmaker said. "For me, I just went back in the studio. I’ve written some of the best songs that I’ve ever written, and I’m really excited.

“It’s a very happy-era album. It’s some of the most joyous, beautiful songs that have just a tad of a tear in them," she added.

Her comments come mere weeks after she got candid about her kids going off to college in an emotional social video.

"My kids are going away to college," she said while going through her morning skincare regimen.

The "On the Floor" singer revealed that she made a point of soaking up as much time as possible with Max and Emme over the summer, including traveling with them before they began their new lives away from home.

"I was thinking about this summer and what a great summer it was. We got to go away together. I spent as much time with them as I could," she recalled.

Lopez revealed she was facing the reality of returning to a much quieter home—and admitted that it hasn't been easy.

"When they go away and I'm sitting here being an empty nester, and crying and thinking about them and looking at baby pictures of them and all of that stuff, these routines are the things that are going to keep me kind of sane," she shared.

For Lopez, those routines include exercising, taking care of her skin, and making an effort to prioritize herself as she navigates the newfound free time that comes with having two college-age children.

"Working out, doing my skincare routine, caring for myself, with the newfound kind of space that's in your life," she said.

But the superstar also acknowledged that the milestone comes with conflicting emotions. While she is thrilled to watch Max and Emme begin their adult lives, their departure also marks a major change for her.

"You're so excited for them to step into this new era of their life, but it's also, we have to remember, it's a new era of our lives, too," Lopez explained.

She encouraged other parents experiencing a similar transition to look at the change as an opportunity to reconnect with interests or ambitions that may have taken a back seat while raising children.

"Maybe it's time to revive some old dreams that you had," she suggested, adding that parents might return to something they "put aside during the time that you were raising your kids" or simply pursue activities they previously didn't have time for.

Still, Lopez didn't shy away from admitting that embracing such a significant lifestyle change can be daunting.

"It's a scary time. It's a transitional time. It's a new beginning, in a lot of ways, for them, certainly, but also for you," she said.

She ended her message on an optimistic note, urging others entering the empty-nest phase to continue looking after themselves and finding purpose in their new routines.

"Keep your routines going. Stay hydrated. Stay happy, stay joyful, stay productive," she said. Lopez has been preparing for the milestone for months.

Earlier this year, she revealed during an interview with "Extra" that both Max and Emme had been accepted into all five colleges they applied to, with each also receiving a scholarship offer.

The proud mom also spoke about how hard the twins had worked to reach that point, explaining that both have ADHD and have had to find approaches to learning that work for them.

Lopez also made sure to carve out plenty of time with her children before their departure. Over the summer, she documented a road trip through Italy with Max and Emme.

#5528. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5527. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5526. Inside the Properties James Bond Has Made Famous as Robert Pattinson Gears Up to Play 007

It’s official: Robert Pattinson is stepping into the role of James Bond.

The news comes after years of speculation surrounding who might succeed Daniel Craig—who was the sixth actor to bring 007 to life, and portrayed the British spy in five films, ending with 2021’s “No Time To Die.”

The official James Bond X account shared a first look of Pattinson donning the infamous tux for the role, captioned “Identity Confirmed.”

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Director Denis Villeneuve alluded to the search for the next Bond in the statement.

“I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” the “Dune” director said. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007.”

Dozens of potential candidates have been floated as possibilities since Craig’s reign came to an end, including Idris Elba, Jacob Elordi, Callum Turner, and John Hardy.

Bond first walked onto the silver screen in 1962, when Sean Connery brought the iconic book character to life in the first film, “Dr. No.” There have been a whopping 25 Bond films so far, with Pattinson suiting up for the 26th.

After seven films, Connery ended his run in 1983 with “Never Say Never.” In 1969, George Lazenby became the only actor to star in a single film in the franchise, with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.”

Roger Moore held the role from 1973 to 1985, also impressively holding the gig for seven titles. Next up was Timothy Dalton, who starred in two films between 1987 and 1989.

Pierce Brosnan reinvigorated the franchise when he became Bond in 1995, holding the job until 2002. In 2006, Craig ushered in a new era, tackling 007 with a more rough-and-tumble edge.

Perhaps even more impressive than the scale of actors who have taken their martinis shaken, not stirred, is the sheer number of filming locations the franchise has made its mark on for over 60 years.

Hunting Bond, a fan site that tracks the locations, has identified nearly 600 filming spots across the world. While the James Bond universe is certainly action-packed, it’s also quite aspirational, and has often provided viewers with rich backgrounds and fascinating properties that became characters in their own right.

It would be nearly impossible to rank all of the lavish homes Bond has stepped foot in over the years, but there are definitely a handful that stand out in memory.

Even without a connection to one of the Bond films with the strongest pop culture staying power—”Diamonds Are Forever,” of course—the Elrod House in Palm Springs, CA, is an incredible dwelling.

Perched on a hillside overlooking Coachella Valley, the 8,900-square-foot home was designed by modernist architect John Lautner for interior designer Arthur Elrod.

The fascinating structure has a concrete dome-shaped roof, a circular living room, and a half-moon swimming pool that Connery’s Bond threw an enemy into during a heated fight scene.

Villa Sylva is a picturesque Greek estate that’s appeared in a handful of movies, including Moore’s “For Your Eyes Only”—although in the film, it assumed the role of the Madrid home of hitman Hector Gonzales.

The 12-bedroom luxury villa boasts unobstructed views of the Ionian Sea and is perched on an idyllic 10-acre property. Today, it can be rented as a wedding venue or a vacation home sleeping up to 18 people.

Given Bond’s important role at the UK-based M16, it only makes sense that at least some of the locations had to be local. The sprawling Luton Hoo Estate was a location in Brosnan’s 1999 film, “The World Is Not Enough” and Connery’s 1983 return for “Never Say Never Again.”

It’s also been featured in dozens of other projects, including “Downton Abbey.”

Built in 1903, the property is about an hour’s drive from London—a journey that would probably be cut in half when Bond is behind the wheel. The historic English country estate spans more than 1,000 acres and has a handful of structures—most notably, a five-star hotel and an exquisite mansion.

Craig’s Bond debut in the 2006 film, “Casino Royale,” was set in the breathtaking Ocean Club in the Bahamas.

The luxury resort has a number of sea-view villas for rent, including one that served as the perfect backdrop for a romantic scene between the spy and Solange Dimitrios, the wife of villain Alex Dimitrios.

Although Bond was just a visitor, the Ocean Club does have “67 turnkey oceanfront residences” available for ownership. The ultraprivate oceanfront abodes are available in a variety of sizes between two- and five-bedroom. Pricing begins at $7.5 million, according to the Ocean Club’s website.

It’s never been captured on screen in a Bond film, but 007 creator Ian Fleming built a bungalow called GoldenEye in Port Antonio, Jamaica.

The private estate is where the prolific author wrote all 13 of the original James Bond novels. Eventually, it was sold and turned into a resort, which is still called GoldenEye today. The property has been vastly expanded in the decades since Fleming, who died in 1964, lived there. It now includes lagoon cottages, villas, beach huts, and a spa.

The 25th Bond film, “No Time To Die,” provided a nod to the character’s birthplace. According to Architectural Digest, there’s a replica of Fleming’s desk in the opening scene of the film. Like the writer, Bond lives in a Jamaican bungalow in this installation, but it was built from scratch solely for filming.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5525. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

#5523. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

#5522. Aging Parents and Empty Nests Force Homeowners To Rethink Layouts Years Before the Move

Most homeowners know their homes may need updates to accommodate their changing needs as they age.

Some, however, are thinking even further ahead.

Instead of waiting until those changes are necessary, they’re investing in renovations years in advance to prepare for aging parents who might eventually move in after their children leave the nest.

Angi’s 2026 State of Home Spending Pulse study found that 66% of homeowners plan to make a major home investment within the next five years. And the 2027 Home Trends To Watch report predicts that 2027 will be the year they take a proactive approach and focus on creating a home that grows with them.

If you own your home, experts agree that you should anticipate how your needs could change in the next five to 10 years and use that information to guide your long-term home improvement goals today.

By doing so, you can make the most out of your renovation budget, avoid costly last-minute adjustments, and ensure your home comfortably adapts to the different stages of life.

Matt Plaskoff, CEO and founder of One Week Bath in Los Angeles, is seeing this proactive, multigenerational "future-proofing” trend among his clients.

“It comes down to people having heard stories of it going the other way. Mom falls or receives a diagnosis, and suddenly the family is trying to put in a walk-in shower and grab bars on short notice while suddenly incurring more costs with doctors and insurance,” says Plaskoff.

Multigenerational living is also at an all-time high, and the recent National Association of Realtors® Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers report reflects this shift. It found that 17% of homes purchased last year were intended for multigenerational households.

And when adult kids leave, there’s suddenly more space that makes it easier to create a home that works well for both aging in place and aging parents.

We can’t forget the housing affordability crisis forcing families to rethink the homes they already own.

“The house may no longer fit the household, but buying a better-fitting home can mean a higher price, a higher mortgage rate, and higher monthly expenses,” says Jon Brooks, co-founder of Momentum Realty in Jacksonville, FL.

Plus, it's more cost-effective to future-proof your home when you plan properly and actually have the funds to support your projects.

“The worst time to remodel is when you don’t have the budget for it. You make decisions that should take time and careful planning under pressure and may just accept whatever contractor can show up ASAP, even if it means you have to pay more,” says Plaskoff.

If you're already opening up walls for a bath remodel, for example, adding blocking for future grab bars, widening a doorway, or adding a curbless shower will be faster and cheaper than if you were to come back later and redo finished work.

Experts agree that a strong universal design features a functional yet beautiful bathroom with a wider doorway, good lighting, lever handles for knobs, a walk-in shower, and slip-resistant flooring.

“If done right, it feels more like a spa than a hospital, and that’s what matters most to those who are using it every day,” Plaskoff explains.

You might also consider adding a second structure to your backyard like an accessory dwelling unit or tiny home.

“For families with the space, an ADU is one of the best solutions we see. It gives an aging parent true independence, with their own kitchen, bath, and front door, while keeping them close enough for daily connection and support,” explains Michelle Squire, designer and principal at Studio SQUARE in San Francisco.

If long-term resale is important to you, be sure to consider what buyers value in your neighborhood. This way you can determine where to make permanent changes and where to keep things flexible.

“If you’re overimproving for the area, just understand you may have a harder time recouping that money if you choose to sell,” says Christina Rordam, real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando, FL.

At the end of the day, prioritize flexibility, try not to over improve for the neighborhood you’re in, and most importantly, consider what works best for you and your family.

#5521. Sellers Vastly Outnumber Buyers as Top Metros Shift Further: Report

Buying house, real estate deal and investment. Tiny woman carrying money in shopping cart to buy family home, agent or broker giving building model and apartment key cartoon vector illustration

Sellers have largely had the upper-hand in the housing market since the pandemic as home prices reached new peaks, giving sellers max equity to see large returns on their investments. Now, as the market is observing some shifts, a new report from Redfin found that seller’s markets are losing ground.

Homebuyers have gained more negotiating power across the country, as Redfin data estimated there were 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October. This was the biggest recorded gap seen since 2013, as well as the sixth month in a row this measure has reached a new record.

Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan said that sellers are “increasingly competing for buyers’ attention,” which has led to more “price reductions, concessions and other savings.”

“First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle—but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate,” he continued. “With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting—and can afford today’s costs—may have an opportunity to make a move.”

Looking at the 50 most populous metros in the U.S., only three were seller’s markets in October. Redfin used “proprietary” data on buyer behavior and MLS listings to estimate the balance of buyers and sellers.

Notably, all three of the seller’s markets were located in the Northeast, where home prices remain higher than other regions. These three markets saw home prices rise 3.3% year-over-year in October, compared to prices increasing only 0.3% in buyer’s markets.

The top of the three seller’s markets was Nassau County, New York, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers, a gap that actually shrank from 28.3% the month prior. The other two markets were Newark, New Jersey (14.3% fewer sellers, down from 17.6% the month prior) and Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (12.1% fewer sellers, down from 20.1% the month prior).

Another difference from September’s data was the loss of a fourth seller’s market—Milwaukee, Wisconsin, which is now balanced between buyers and sellers.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says one real estate professional. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.” Read more.

#5520. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Szu Yu Chen is a senior data visualization designer and developer who creates interactive graphics and data-driven experiences. Previously, she worked as a graphics reporter at The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times.

#5519. La Gorce Island Point Lot Overlooking Biscayne Bay Is Listed for an Eye-Watering $170 Million

A spectacular waterfront mansion on Miami’s guard-gated La Gorce Island has hit the market for a jaw-dropping $170 million.

Built in 2015, the legacy estate is reportedly owned by Betsy Sherman, wife of George Sherman, the late former chairman of Campbell’s. If the property fetches anywhere near its asking price, it would rank among Miami’s most expensive home sales ever, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The Shermans purchased the property for just $17 million in 2006 and custom-built the sprawling 18,213-square-foot estate, which now claims the top spot on the Realtor.com® weekly list of the most expensive homes.

Boasting 320 feet of Biscayne Bay frontage, the residence was designed to capture spectacular sunset views from nearly every room.

Interior highlights include an expansive great room with sliding glass doors that open to the outdoor living area, a formal dining room, a modern kitchen, and a bar.

A sculptural, curved glass staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, where a lavish primary retreat features a private terrace overlooking the bay.

Additional amenities include a fitness center, bunk room, pool, four-car garage, and deep-water dock designed to accommodate yachts.

More spectacular mansions to make the week's most expensive homes list include a Utah mountain retreat under construction, an oceanfront estate in Hawaii with sweeping Pacific Ocean views, and a rebuilt Palm Beach, FL, sanctuary.

Gold Coast: This 50-foot-wide double lot on the north side of Broadway has panoramic views from San Francisco Bay and the Golden Gate Bridge to Alcatraz and the Marin Headlands.

Built in 1908, the seven-bedroom estate was reconstructed in 2007 and has 9,001 square feet of reimagined space. The four-level home has herringbone-patterned floors, arched doorways, built-in bookshelves, custom millwork, seven fireplaces, and an elevator to each floor. A stained-glass skylight illuminates the sculptural staircase.

The formal living room is surrounded by floor-to-ceiling windows framing the waterfront views. The professional-grade kitchen, with a butler’s pantry and breakfast bar, flows into the dining room, which has patio access. The lower level has a wine cellar, a secondary laundry room, service areas, and storage space.

A private sport court is surrounded by mature greenery.

Neal Ward of Compass is the listing agent.

Teardown opportunity: This 2.33-acre property offers a rare chance to “create a dream estate on a truly grand scale.”

Built in 1959, the existing nine-bedroom home has 16,290 square feet of space. Offered “with the freedom to build from the ground up,” the property is in the country’s most expensive ZIP code and near the tech hubs of Silicon Valley. No interior photos are included with the listing, but it does show a swimming pool.

The expansive lot has room for gardens and large-scale entertaining.

Ken Deleon of Deleon Realty is the listing agent.

Fjell House: This 11,632-square-foot mountain retreat will be the largest new home in the gated Stein Eriksen Estates in Deer Valley when it is completed in 2027.

The seven-bedroom home will also have 3,567 square feet of outdoor living space. Interior highlights will include a great room with a 12-foot ceiling, an entertainer’s kitchen with a quartzite waterfall island, a spacious dining room, a home office, and dual primary suites, each with its own deck and fireplace.

A white oak floating staircase will descend to the lower level, which will have a lounge, a bar, a 172-bottle wine storage system, a golf and sports room, a fitness center with a teak sauna, three guest suites, and a bunk room with access to a patio with an eight-person hot tub and fire pit.

The home will also have an oversized three-car garage with EV-charging capabilities.

Kristen Barber of Stein Eriksen Realty Group is the listing agent.

Old Marsh Golf Club: This legacy compound, set on 1.77 lakefront acres, has a primary residence, a guest cottage, a separate apartment, and a seven-car garage.

The eight-bedroom estate has marble and wood flooring, coffered ceilings, four fireplaces, a commercial elevator, built-ins, and French doors that open to spacious patios.

Other amenities include four fully equipped kitchens, a primary suite with dual dressing rooms and separate baths, a 3,000-bottle wine gallery, an entertainment room, and a bar. Covered patios overlook mature banyan trees, manicured gardens, and a swimming pool.

The property also has access to a Pete Dye championship course, regarded for its no-tee-time policy and renowned caddie program.

Jim McCann of Premier Estate Properties is the listing agent.

The Bluffs at Mauna Kea Resort: Set in an enclave of just 11 oceanfront residences, this five-bedroom estate sits on a promontory with more than 200 feet of ocean frontage.

Overlooking Mauna Kea and Hapuna beaches, the nearly 1-acre lot on Hawai’i’s Kohala Coast is surrounded by Pacific Ocean views. Built in 2004, the 9,909-square-foot home was “refined over six years” by Mexican architects Ricardo and Victor Legorreta, with living spaces designed around light, color, and water.

Glass walls and lanais connect the indoor living areas with the coastal setting. A sunken courtyard with a black stone water feature is surrounded by patios for entertaining and enjoying the views.

The property also has a two-car garage and access to nearby golf, beaches, and dining.

Harold Clarke of Luxury Big Island is the listing agent.

The Light House: This newly built waterfront estate is owned by powerboat racer and real estate investor Ross Romash and his wife, Caroline Romash, who bought the property for $2.45 million in 2021.

The double-height great room has disappearing glass walls that transform the space into a waterfront pavilion. The 11,358-square-foot interior includes a “showpiece” kitchen with a waterfall island and a hidden pantry, a primary suite with a water-facing terrace, and a glass-enclosed fitness center with a private poolside entrance and a bay-view sauna.

Intracoastal Waterway views: This seven-bedroom waterfront estate offers 1.88 acres of seclusion, complete with a private beach area.

Floor-to-ceiling glass walls frame sweeping views of Biscayne Bay, while formal and casual living, dining, and entertaining spaces are found throughout the home. Upstairs, an ornate primary suite features a private bay-facing terrace, accompanied by four en suite bedrooms.

The property also boasts a wellness center with a gym, sauna, steam room, and cold plunge. Covered terraces overlook the pool and private boat dock.

Elyse Taylor of Mocca Realty is the listing agent.

The extensively restored interior features a bright, airy open floor plan framed by sweeping waterfront views. Outside, formal gardens and expansive lawns lead to 165.9 feet of Intracoastal Waterway frontage.

Suzanne Trapani- Frisbie of The Corcoran Group is the listing agent.

La Gorce Island: This eight-bedroom waterfront estate is reportedly owned by Betsy Sherman, wife of George Sherman, the late former chairman of the Campbell’s Company.

Built in 2015, the 18,213-square-foot mansion occupies a prominent point lot at the tip of the island, with 320 feet of open Biscayne Bay frontage. Designed to capture waterfront views from nearly every room, the property was customized for both grand entertaining and intimate waterfront living.

Highlights include a primary retreat with a bayfront balcony, a living room with retractable glass walls, and a chef’s kitchen with access to a covered terrace. A floating circular staircase leads to an upstairs primary suite overlooking the bay and pool.

The 1.23-acre property also features a four-car garage and a deep-water dock capable of accommodating large yachts.

Jill Hertzberg of Coldwell Banker Realty is the listing agent.

#5518. Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

The October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.
