#5500. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5499. Exec: Time for Banks to Reclaim Mortgage Biz From Non-Bank Lenders

Mortgage rates recently reached 7.51% on the 30-year fixed, almost a full percentage point higher than last year. Despite that, the CEO of Chase Home Lending plans to aggressively expand its mortgage business to reclaim market share from non-bank lenders.

In a recent report on CNBC, Sean Grzebin noted that while banks had to recover consumer confidence following the great financial crisis of 20-some years ago, he thinks that’s a done deal.

“The non-banks are all very formidable competitors, and I think they’ve had an advantage while the banks were distracted through several decades,” he said. “Now you’re starting to see the resurgence of banks. A lot of banks are actually going to grow their mortgage business through this.”

Some of the major non-bank lenders in the U.S. include Rocket Mortgage, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), PennyMac Loan Services, loanDepot, Better Mortgage, to name a few.

Non-banks currently dominate originations with a 66.3% share by dollar volume, up from just 27% before the 2008 financial crisis, according to CNBC. However, large banks with $50 billion or more in assets are now increasing originations by 34% annually, outperforming competitors.

“We’re going to hire a bunch of lending advisors across the United States,” said Grzebin. “We’re going to focus on areas where we haven’t had a lot of coverage, but there’s a lot of mortgage activity and transactions taking place. And it really matches the expansion that we’re having within the branch network on the consumer bank side.”

Non-banks had a 66.3% share of originations by dollar volume in the first half of this year, an increase over all of 2025, according to Inside Mortgage Finance. That compares with just a 27% share in 2000 before the financial crisis. But large banks, those with $50 billion and more in assets, are now increasing originations by 34% on an annual basis, outperforming both competing banks and non-banks.”

#5498. AT&T uses agentic AI to reinvent business processes from the ground up

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin

AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant plans to triple that number next year.

AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin said the company’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

At the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin said.

One early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually update records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the company maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin said.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin said production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

A 151-year-old company that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin said. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”

Sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin said. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”

Encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he said.

Corbin said AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support new sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin said responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

“I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he said. “What we do should be completely distributed.”

#5497. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5496. Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications

Swedish application security company Detectify AB today launched Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabilities can be exploited in running applications.

A new Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test. Detectify is pitching the release at DevSecOps teams that are unsure whether they can trust what their AI agents report.

Detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise. Under pressure to deliver an answer, an agent can also produce a convincing report about a test it never ran, the company warned.

Even before AI agents enter the picture, many security teams are falling behind. Nine in 10 open critical and high-severity vulnerabilities had stayed exposed for more than 90 days, according to Detectify’s H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index. In a study by researchers at Fudan University and Tencent Holdings Ltd., 76% of the static-analysis alerts examined were found to be false positives. Each one took developers 10 to 20 minutes to review.

Through Agentic Tooling, agents can tap the testing engines Detectify has built over more than a decade. Included are payload assessments sourced from its ethical hacker community, attack surface data from its Surface Monitoring product and Alfred, an AI system the company launched in March 2025 to automate tests for known vulnerabilities.

Running in a customer’s own environment, the tools connect to agents through either the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface. They operate only on the data a customer provides and are said to work with whichever agent the customer already uses.

At the center of the design is loop engineering, an emerging practice of running AI agents in automated, repeating workflows rather than prompting them by hand. Kicking off each loop is a trigger such as a continuous integration run. Whether it comes from a code scan, a bug bounty report, a red team or Detectify’s own attack surface data, each finding is turned into a ticket.

Once an agent picks up a ticket, it reads the relevant code before testing the live application from the outside, as an attacker would. Run continuously, the loop becomes what Detectify calls a verification factory.

The requests sent, the payloads used and the results returned are all logged in the Security Ledger each time an agent uses Detectify’s tools. Written by Detectify rather than the agent, the append-only ledger lets teams separate findings backed by actual tests from unsupported AI conclusions. Any ticket that could cause harm, such as a denial-of-service test, is marked unsafe for a person to decide on.

“Ask an agent to write your code, then ask the same agent whether it’s secure. If it says yes, you don’t actually know,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson. There are plenty of examples of agents fabricating proof to please the person asking, according to Carlsson, who described Detectify’s aim as “building proof that an agent can’t fabricate.”

Available on request starting today, Agentic Tooling builds on the Detectify MCP Server that the company announced in May to give AI agents access to its security findings. Investors include Insight Partners, which took a majority stake in October 2024, along with Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy and SquareOne App Ltd.
